subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

speechtext:
ISO. Departmental administration, $287,000.
. Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare): Mr. Chairman, as this is the first time the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare have come before the committee I think it
Supply

Health and Welfare

might be convenient to hon. members if I described briefly the organization and functions of the department.
It was created by the Department of National Health and Welfare Act, chapter 22, statutes of 1944, which received ro^al assent on July 27, 1944. That act was proclaimed on October 13, when I Was appointed its first minister. The department took over the health branch of the department of pensions and national health. That department had been created in 1928, when the old department of health and the department of soldiers' civil reestablishment were amalgamated. The department of health itself was created in 1919.
When the Department of National Health and Welfare was created on October 13, 1944, the health branch of the department of health and pensions, which was taken over, had a total personnel of 387. At that time the new department had no administrative staff whatever, and no staff in the welfare branch. It was a time, as hon. members know, of great shortages of space and personnel, and at first the work of the department had to be organized from offices in the House of Com' mans. Later the administration has been carried on from offices in the Birks building, and only now, more than a jrear after its creation, is the department being gradually assembled in one place, in offices in the Jackson building.
The health branch had a number of different functions. It administered many acts of this parliament which went back even to preconfederation days. I might list them for the convenience of hon. members:
(a)	The Foods and Drugs Act;
(b)	The Opium and Narcotics Act;
(c)	The Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act;
(d)	The Quarantine Act;
(e)	The Leprosy Act. The health branch also furnished services with regard to
(f)	Maternal and child hygiene;
(g)	The examination of immigrants;
(h)	Nutrition;
(i)	Public health engineering; for example, public works health service; public health on railways, steamships, et cetera, and particular jobs such as water supply at military camps;
(j)	Sick mariners service, which since confederation has provided medical and surgical treatment to members of crews of vessels in the classes specified in the Canada Shipping Act. In addition the department makes certain grants to institutions to assist sailors;
(k)	Venereal disease control, including assistance to the provinces, coordination of various controls, the distribution of drugs used in veneral disease treatment;

(l)	Administration of the laboratory of
hygiene, including testing and establishing of standards for food and drugs, standardization of reagent^, studying sources of vitamins, et cetera;	[DOT]
(m)	Control of food and drug advertising and labelling;
(n)	Cooperation with other governments in the administration of sanitary conventions, et cetera.
These functions had been carried on, as I say, by the health branch of the department of pensions and national health, and they were taken over by the new department. Since then a number of new developments have taken place, particularly during the last year, and new divisions have been created to deal with the following matters:
1.	Health insurance studies, the purpose of which is to extend the studies that have been carried on by this department and by parliamentary committees in the past.
2.	Dental health.
3.	Civil servants' health. That was announced in May, 1945, in consequence of authorization being given by the government to supply a service to civil servants which would put the Dominion of Canada on a footing with other good employers with regard to the health service to be furnished to the civil service, including examination on entrance, periodical examinations, X-ray examinations, emergency treatment, advice on health matters and education on health matters.
4.	Health facilities. This division is designed to supply advice and information to government departments, to provincial governments and to other agencies with regard to hospital construction. At present there are not a great number of architects qualified to supply consultative advice and assistance in connection with the construction of hospitals, and we feel it is desirable to have such a man with the required knowledge and to equip him and make his services available to other agencies interested in using them. This course was taken in accordance with a resolution of the Dominion Council of Health.
5.	Mental health.
6.	Blindness control. The proposals made by the dominion government to the provinces provide for extending the age at which blindness will be pensionable from forty down to twenty-one, and also, in cooperation with the provinces for both preventive and curative services to the blind. We hope almost at once to undertake a survey of the files and medical records of blind people in Canada registered

Supply-Health and Welfare
with the department so as to arrive at exact statistical knowledge of the different causes of blindness and ascertain how much of it is preventable or curable. On the basis of that information we can start some really constructive work in that field.
7.	Tuberculosis control.
8.	Advertising and labelling control. The purpose of this division would be to coordinate the work previously done in several divisions of the department and cooperate much more actively with those engaged in the pharmaceutical trade, the advertising agencies and others interested in this field, in order to arrive at standards of medicine and health advertising which will be thoroughly understood and readily applied.
9.	National laboratory. Last May I was also authorized to announce that we would plan to have a national laboratory in Canada which would, we hoped, put Canada on a footing with any other country in the world, and which would provide us with the last word in laboratory equipment to conduct the public health business of the dominion. This building is being planned now. It is expected that construction will not begin for some considerable time, but when it is in being we hope it will be something of which the Canadian people can be proud.
In addition to these new divisions which have been created, during the year the department has undertaken a number of other activities. It now publishes the Canadian Health and Welfare Bulletin, which is distributed free to provincial governments, public health authorities and others engaged in that field. The distribution amounts to 50,000 copies in English and 25,000 copies in French. Already it has had a very good reception. It takes the place of a bulletin previously issued by the department, and represents hardly any increase in cost. The department is also working with other government agencies to develop a film library on health matters and also to develop a very much more complete public health and welfare library. In time we hope to be able to provide the provinces and other agencies in the field with information in regard to everything going on in these fields in other countries as well as in every part of Canada, and in this way serve the interests of the provinces and all others concerned. On November 1 the hospitalization and medical treatment of Indians was transferred to the department, but my colleague the Minister of Mines and Resources will include the presentation of those items in his estimates, because since
November 1 we have not had time to take them over. We greatly appreciate his courtesy in this respect.
In the general health field, since the department was created we have endeavoured to get into dose personal relationship with the ministers and department of health of the provinces and with all the agencies working in this field, such as the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Dental Association, the Health League of Canada, the Canadian Institute for the Blind, the Canadian Nurses' Association, the Red Cross, and a number of others. I am happy to say that all have not only expressed their desire to cooperate but have given every indication of a genuine wish to cooperate in the great work of improving the 'health and welfare of the Canadian people.
I should say a word about the organization of the welfare department. It started out on October 13 of last year, as I said, with no staff, no quarters, no equipment, and it was faced with the task of seeing that the children of Canada were registered and that cheques were issued by the month of July. There were times when I thought we could not possibly meet that goal, but the thing got going; we commenced the registration of families in Prince Edward Island in February and gained very valuable experience there before undertaking the job of registration in all the provinces, which commenced on March 22 of 1945. At that time we did not even have office space in two of the provinces, and as the forms came in they had to be stored temporarily. In the connection I should like to express a wrarm word of gratitude to the hundreds if not thousands of volunteer workers in 6very part of Canada who helped in the work of sorting the forms and generally in the preliminaries of registration. These women were obtained largely through the women's voluntary agencies; many were office women who voluntarily contributed their free services after office hours so that this job of national importance might be done in time.
We were able to make the first payment on July 18 as planned; payments have been made in respect of the months of July, August, September, October and November. The November payment was made about the 18th of the month, and we already have the figures in regard to that payment, which I am prepared to give the committee. It was made in respect of 1,393,546 families and amounted to a total of 819,722,599. The size of this operation I think may be understood when I say that in the month of October alone we had 40,331 changes of address and 92250 automatic
Supply-Health and Welfare

changes occasioned by the children moving from one age level to another. These automatic changes are made without any action on the part of the parent; they are made from the information we have on file, and are done by changing the address slugs and other equipment used to send out cheques.
The work of registration has been greatly facilitated by the simple form we ultimately selected after a great deal of trial. If you compare the form used in Canada with that in use in Australia or New Zealand or Ireland I think you will see that we have by far the simplest form. We have found that it gives adequate information, and by reason of the cooperation of the Canadian people and the amount of publicity that was given, a large percentage of' the forms were properly filled out, although delays in payment have occurred in a considerable number of cases through the forms not being properly filled out. For example, some thousands of forms were sent in with no addresses on them. The applicants inadvertently left off the addresses, and we had no means of communicating with them until they wrote in again. Then we had tp relate the form to the letter and see that the cheques were mailed in payment. There have been delays, but I think those delays are almost entirely caught up now. They were due to shortages of space, shortages of staff in practically every province, and considerable shortages of equipment arising from delays in obtaining the machinery and office furniture. But to-day in every province except Quebec applications are dealt with the day they are received, and generally speaking correspondence is replied to the following day. In Quebec that is generally true with regard to current applications and correspondence, but there is. still a relatively small backlog of correspondence which we hope to catch up with in the next week, and which will put the whole operation on an absolutely current basis. When it is considered that already six and a half million cheques have been issued and that these delays probably do not affect one-tenth of one per cent of the total it is a record of which the men and women who have worked night and day in the regional offices may well be proud.
This work has been greatly facilitated, and indeed I think was possible only by reason of the very fine cooperation we have received from other government departments. I should like to pay tribute to the accuracy of the estimates made by the dominion bureau of statistics, on which all our calculations and organization had to be based. We had to determine through one means or another, 
sometimes through the post oflice and sometimes through other agencies, how many forms in French or in English would have to be available in each part of Canada and in each post office in Canada. It should be remembered that we delivered the forms to households, in French or English according to the language of the householder, so that people did not even have to call for their forms unless there had been some failure in delivery. In arriving at the size of the staff and at the quantity of equipment we had to have very accurate estimates. The dominion bureau of statistics made these estimates on the basis of the 1941 census projected to July, 1945, and they were extraordinarily accurate. We have a statistical service which is not only a great credit to those responsible for it but is essential if an operation of this kind is to be carried on. Also the treasury officials, who have done great work, and the post . office and the provincial governments as well as the municipal authorities cooperated generously in seeing that this very considerable operation was carried out on time.
It should be remembered that we have had only four months of operation and have been dealing with fifteen years of backlog of children, so that we have not got down to a month-to-month basis. When the bill was being debated in July, 1944, I gave the house an estimate of the cost of family allowance administration in the Department of National Health and Welfare itself; I said we thought it would run not higher than two per cent, and closer to one per cent. I am glad to say that our estimate or guess was well within the limits of actuality; it looks now as if we shall be able to get through the first year with a cost of one per cent and in future years at considerably less. The estimate of staff I made at that time was that we should have 500 in the offices; at present we have 450, with a considerable additional number of casual employees who have been there to take care of the peak load. It may be that we shall need, when the operation settles down, rather more than 500, but it is still too early to say that. On the other hand I said that we would need a field force of 500, and we shall certainly not need anything like that figure. I said that the number of treasury officials would likely total 600; on November 14 they totalled 583. So that generally speaking the estimates were sound, and the aim we set for ourselves at that time has been bettered.

Supply-Health and Welfare
We decided, after considering the whole subject, that this job could be done only with complete decentralization. Family allowance registrations were made in respect of the children in each province, and the family allowance office where they were made was in the capital of each province. Cheques were issued from that regional office at the capital, and the correspondence was conducted from there. That permitted us to do this very large job of organization. We could not have done it in time had we tried to do it at Ottawa. For one thing, the mails would have been swamped at the end of each month. The total family allowance staff at headquarters in Ottawa totals the rather extraordinary figure of seven.
During the year, in accordance with the intentions expressed when the department was established, the administration of the old age pensions branch, which had been with the Department of Finance, was transferred to the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The department like other departments of government, was also occupied during a considerable part of the year in working on studies which led to the proposals of the dominion government which were put before the dominion-provincial conference. The proposals regarding health and welfare matters will be found in the green book, as we call it. That contains the proposals of the dominion government, set out at length. I will not refer to them except to mention that those with regard to health include:
(a)	A grant for planning.
(b)	A system of health insurance on a nation-wide basis to the administered by the provinces, to which the federal government would contribute approximately sixty per cent of the cost, which would give Canadians in every part of Canada complete health service.
(c)	A programme of health grants under eight different heads, which would total some 813,000,000 and which would provide a very much larger sum, through provincial contributions to be spent on public health measures as well as on preventive and curative medicine.
(d)	Assistance in the construction of hospitals whereby provincial and municipal authorities could borrow money at cost.
These proposals also include the change in the provision for the blind, which I have mentioned, and also a change in old age pensions whereby an old age pension of $30 a month would be payable to everyone in Canada without proof of need at the age of seventy and a similar pension would be payable to those needing it, between the ages
of sixty-five and sixty-nine. The proposals with regard to old age pensions would cost the federal government about $217,000,000 a year, and the proposals with regard to health, if fully implemented, would cost the federal government something like $160,000,000 a year. These proposals are before the provinces now and are receiving their consideration.
That, Mr. Chairman, completes this brief statement of the activities and organization of the department. This department is, I believe, the only one which is by statute charged with responsibility for seeing to the health and welfare of the Canadian people in the federal field, and I believe I am the only minister who is by statute expressly charged with responsibility for seeing to it that these two ingredients of human happiness, health and welfare, shall be attended to in so far as it is within our power. We have been conscious of that responsibility, and we are conscious also of the fact that we have not made along every line the progress we should have liked to make. But in view of the times and of the transition from war to peacq, I feel that the officers and employees of the department have reason to congratulate themselves on a good first year. I hope they will feel encouraged by the results so far obtained and that on the foundations laid in this first year we shall be able to build the health and welfare of the Canadian people.
I should like to say a further word in appreciation of the splendid staff in the old health branch of the Department of Pensions and National Health which, when transferred to me from the Minister of Veterans Affairs, we found to be staffed with a group of public servants whose devotion to the public service and the welfare of Canada it would be hard to exceed. They have fitted into the new organization and we are now, we believe, a well integrated unit, and can build on the foundation already laid.
I believe that health and welfare are two matters in which all hon. members of this house, irrespective of party, and every person in the country, are vitally interested. We have had nothing but the best of cooperation from everyone. I believe that cooperation will still be forthcoming, and it is in that spirit that I lay these estimates before the committee for its consideration.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister one matter which he did not deal with in his factual and interesting resume of the affairs of his department, which, as he says, is entirely removed from the question of partisanship. During the past twenty-five years there has been a 'marked extension of health services and in improvement of conditions of those why by reason of disabilities of one kind and another are unable to enjoy the standard of living which we believe is the minimum for all. 'While much has been done in the matter of old age pensions, there is still much more to be done. Pensions for the blind, family allowances, and the like have been provided but there is one section of our population which faces difficulties that ought not to exist.
I refer to those who while not blind are physically crippled. All of us know of persons who by reason of congenital crippleness or as a result of accidents are unable to carry

on and therefore become a charge on their relatives. Often those relatives are unable to carry on and furnish themselves with the proper standard of living. I do not know the extent to which the minister has statistics on this matter, but it would be of interest to find out how many throughout the dominion are cripples and therefore unable to earn a living. A number of the crippled have formed themselves into organizations and memorialized the minister and communicated with hon. members. I think this is a field which has been neglected. I do not want to go into individual cases, but instances have come to the attention of all of us of the breadwinner, sustaining injury under such circumstances that there is no right of recovery under the provincial workmen's compensation act, and certainly no right of recovery under common law. There is no provision for persons in that category. I shall not discuss in detail the project which has been placed before hon. members in this regard, except to say that the requests made seem to be reasonable. In more than nine other countries provision is made for persons in this category. One can never hope to give them the standard of living that they would have if they had the full use of their faculties, but at least something should be done.
I am not making any emotional appeal in this regard. Any one of us could do that, but something should be done to assist these people. I place before you, sir, the project in general, which is this: In addition to the question of hospitalization, which is being dealt with in the provinces, they suggest that crutches, splints and so forth be supplied to those who can move around, and wheel chairs to those where treatment has failed, in order to give them an opportunity to earn at least a partial living under our competitive system. They ask that classes be set up with specially trained teachers in trades or handicrafts. We are more proud of the training which the Department of Veterans Affairs has given to amputation cases from the armed fqrces, thus enabling them with dignity to take their part in the battle for life without any suggestion of charity, which so many resent.
I think that without any unnecessary expenditure in connection with setting up new facilities, new structures and the like, the plan followed by the Department of Veterans Affairs is one which might very well be extended to cripples in civilian life. To begin with, in my view some opportunity should be given to civilians to take advantage of the courses which to-day are being given to veterans.

Supply-Health and Welfare
Finally, we have recognized the principle that persons who are working under severe physical handicaps and are unable to earn a fair living are entitled to pension allowances. Pensions are paid' to the aged, and there is the scheme of family allowances in respect of the young. Consideration should now be given by the department to the extension of pension privileges to those who, by reason of physical disablement are unable to carry on and to acquire financial resources. I would ask the minister to give the committee the benefit of his views in this connection, and an estimate as to the cost of such a project on the basis of statistics available to him, with pensions being paid at a rate similar to that paid to-day in respect of old age pensions.
As I indicated a minute ago, this is the kind of submission concerning which one must be restrained. It requires consideration of a state of affairs in every part of Canada which has led to the existence of conditions we should not permit. The suggestion I make is one which I am sure the people of Canada as a whole would support, in the belief that it is necessary to the well-being of this very considerable portion of our population.

speechtext:
I wish to commend the minister and his department upon the efficient manner in which the family allowances scheme has been put into effect. Members of parliament usually find out whether or not these matters are functioning efficiently and smoothly. I represent a large working class constituency, one in which there are a great many children, and it gives me pleasure to say that I have received only one complaint from that constituency in connection with family allowances.
The committee must realize that the minister is heading a most important department, one which in the years ahead in my opinion will increase in importance and in the work if has to do. We are just beginning to appreciate in Canada the enormous scope of social work which only the federal and the provincial governments can carry out.
Perhaps one of the most satisfactory points the minister brought out was that in regard to the decentralization which has taken place in connection with the administration .of his department. A few weeks ago I had the opportunity of reading the debates which took place in this house and in the other place in 1927 when the Old Age Pensions Act was finally passed. It is amusing to note the expressions of opinion given at that time, particularly in the other place, respecting the extreme dangers involved in passing a measure of the kind-the effect upon the morale of the people of Canada; the taking away .from
the family of the right, duty and obligation to look after such members of the family as were unable to look after themselves. The gentlemen in the other place appeared to be deeply concerned about the dangers implicit in that small excursion into social services. Whether we like it or not, the development of our social and economic system leaves no alternative between that of increasing our social services and leaving large masses of the community unprovided for.
The point made by the hon. member for Lake Centre was well taken. Not only should we provide for persons who have reached the age at which they are eligible for old age pension; we should look after those who, for no reason whatsoever within their control, are unable to earn an income which would permit them to provide their own living. There is no reason why the man or the woman who has reached the age of sixty-nine, sixty-eight or sixty-five, whatever it may be, should have to depend upon charity, if he or she is not able to earn an income, while the person who has reached the age of seventy, as the act now applies, may receive at least a small income which prevents the seeking of charity. Whether we like it or not we shall have to make provision for everyone in the country who is not able, or who for some other reason is prevented, from earning a livelihood. Today this should present no difficulty, because our increased production and our ability to produce wealth in the past few years has so largely increased that we can provide almost an unlimited income.
I am pleased again to commend the minister and his department for the excellent work they have done, particularly in connection with family allowances. I hope we may soon go on to the point at which the department will be in a position to erase from every household in Canada care and worry arising from poverty or inability of the breadwinner to earn an income.

speechtext:
I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre with regard to persons in unfortunate circumstances who, because of trouble or disaster of one kind or another, are unable to do any work. Reports have come to me from lady investigators of the provincial governments respecting many cases which do not fall within that group to which relief measures could be applied. They tell me that these cases are really the most serious they run into in their investigations. There are some who have been bedridden for
Supply-Health and Welfare

years and are a heavy charge upon their families. Some means should be found of giving some //consideration to these people.
I should like to ask the minister if in- connection with his relations with the provincial governments he can undertake some investigation of silicosis. This disease is altogether too prevalent in industries such as moulding shops and rubber factories, and many of the workers end up in a sanatorium. I have no doubt that some investigation has been made, but it should be followed up to see whether some means cannot be worked out of preventing this disease. I commend this as a matter to be investigated by the minister in cooperation with the provincial governments.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to
compliment the minister upon a number of things; first, upon his social vision. There was a time when I feared that the family allowances scheme would have to wait until our own group took office, but I was delighted to see the administration introduce it. I like the method very much; I like the efficiency and the principle upon which the whole thing is operated. I am glad that there are two alternatives open to these families; they can accept the family allowance and return it through income tax if it raises their income beyond a certain limit, or if their income is below that level they can take it without having to give anything back.
The principle of family allowances is sound. The idea of investing in youth is an excellent one, not only from the moral and idealistic point of view, but also from the point of view of actual investment. If we could extend the same principles and vision to the administration of the Old Age Pensions Act we would accomplish a great deal.
The old age pension group is the most pitiful section of our population. I have received many letters from these people, and I know many of them personally.' I know old men who during the last two or three years have almost brought on physical break-downs in their efforts to earn a few dollars to supplement the most inadequate payments on which they are expected to get through the winter. Having made a few dollars in the harvest field, perhaps stooking or attempting in some other way to help bring in the harvest when it was so essential to the war effort, this is the sort of thing they get in their mail boxes:
Dear Sir or Madam:
As a result of improved crop conditions throughout the province, and the consequent improvement in the income of many pensioners,

we are reminding you of the necessity of reporting all income received by you in excess of fifty dollars.
We would like to point out that it is in your own interest to advise us of the receipt of income at the time it is received, and have the pension adjusted immediately, rather than to have us ascertain at a later date that you had excessive income-
These people with an excessive income of $25 per month!
-which would make it necessary for us to suspend your pension to recover -an overpayment at a time when you could ill afford to have your pension suspended.
I have known of old men who earned a few dollars with which they bought victory bonds only to find their pensions reduced, or withheld in full for a short time. This is a shameful condition. If some of these people have the energy and ambition to try to add to the inadequate sums they receive in order to get themselves a little comfort, perhaps a little coal for the winter; in order to pay the rent themselves or to be self-sustaining and regain a little self-respect, it is shameful that we should penalize them like this.
There are few of us who have not some physical ailment as we get older; people rarely reach old age without having illness. There are certain conditions that require treatment. The only province so far that has undertaken to provide for the needs of old age pensioners is the province from which I come, Saskatchewan. I hold in my hand a copy of a blue card which every pensioner received on January 1, last year. This card allows the old age pensioner who is ill to have a doctor, or it admits him to hospital; it supplies him with drugs or appliances like glasses or anything else that he may need. We thought that this was the proper way to provide aid for our pensioners, although we had already added to their pensions to the extent of $3 per month. The pensioners in Saskatchewan all have the advantages of this card, and in addition they have an extra $3 per month,. bringing their pensions up to $28 per month.
Mr. GREEN; Some of the other provinces pay an additional $5 per month.

We provide surgery, drugs, medicine,appliances, and everything the old age pensioner may need without limit. This came into effect on January 1 last year. By the way, we also provide for our widows and dependents. They receive a similar card, except that it is white, which covers the widow and her children.
In addition to providing sufficient income for old age pensioners, I think the time has come when we should do something about the housing of these people. I realize that this subject would more likely come up under housing, but we should recognize that Canada as it stands to-day is the result of the energy, ambition and initiative of these people; that what we have to-day we owe to the men and women who are now in that particular period of their lives. It is only just and natural that we should recognize the great gift that they have given to us. If we intend to put purchasing power in the hands of as many people as possible we cannot afford to keep this section of our population on such a low spending level.
There are other persons who are not covered as yet. I was delighted when the minister submitted the proposal which is now under the consideration of the dominion-provincial con, ference. This is a tribute to the vision of the minister in charge of this department. I am glad that he has departmentalized the assistance that he is asking the provinces to cooperate in providing. The planning and organization grant is an excellent thing. I am glad that he has included general public health, tuberculosis, mental health, venereal diseases, crippled children and all others. In our province we shall immediately be able to take advantage of that tuberculosis grant, and the mental health grant, because we have already made mental health treatment free to our people; and the venereal disease grant, which we have made free, and penicillin, which we supply free to our doctors. But I wish the minister would include cancer, because cancer ranks as a killer away up at the top, second only to heart trouble. We have made the care of cancer completely free to our people, including hospitalization, surgery and all other things such as deep ray and radium that are used in its treatment. I hope that the minister will
include cancer in a separate category along with these other valuable things that he has set out.
But in addition to the people who are covered here, there is one group that we have not yet made provision for, and that is the blind who fall between the ages of sixteen and forty. I understand that the blind pension starts at forty, and the family allowance is cut off at sixteen; so there is a period in the life of a blind person between sixteen and forty years of age when he or she must depend on the care of relatives or go on municipal or provincial relief. Many of them perhaps could be assisted in learning a trade to support themselves. I do not think we should leave it to chance; we should start the pension for the blind where the family allowance leaves off;
Then there are the arthritics. Mention has been made of crippling diseases, but the rapidly increasing rate at which arthritis is spreading demands I think that we give it special attention. It is something that we do not know a lot about. There are a great many theories and a great many suggested treatments, but the painful and extended nature of this disease demands I think special attention. In moving about the country I have been alarmed to notice the number of people you meet who have been in wheel chairs for years and who have suffered incredible pain and are a terrific burden to their family.
I do not think that there is much more that I need to say except this. I wish the minister could see fit to extend to the old age pensioners the same conditions and the same type of administration that is now set up for the family allowance. I wish we could abolish the means test now; I wish we could increase the pension now. We are proud that the level of our family allowance compares so favourably with that paid in other countries. We who have such a rich country, such a big country, such tremendous potentials for production, should be satisfied only when our country leads, not when we approach or favourably compare with other countries. We who have so much should be satisfied only when there is abundance in every home and security for every Canadian regardless of age or condition.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the statement made by the minister of the new Department of National Health and Welfare. Although it did not contain many details which some of us would like to have, I presume he will give these in breaking down the various items for which supply will be voted later on. I understood him to say
*
Supply-Health and Welfare

that sixty per cent of the cost of health insurance would be borne by the federal government, and if so I consider it a very fair proportion.
I did not hear what amount of money would be available for the construction of new hospitals generally throughout the country, and would ask the minister to tell us the amount which will be appropriated for that purpose. Owing to high taxation, excess profits taxes, corporation taxes and succession duties, the money which formerly was available from private sources for hospital construction has to a large extent dried up, and therefore it is up to the federal government to make a considerable contribution for this purpose. The federal government has taken this money from the people so that they are no longer able to make the contributions they formerly did during their lifetime, and they have ceased to make provision in their wills for the construction of hospitals. They think, and quite rightly, that succession duties will take a much larger amount out of their estate and there may be nothing left with which they might otherwise have contributed to such benevolent purposes as the building of hospitals. So I think there is every reason to expect the government to make a very considerable contribution to hospital construction and maintenance. It might very well be done on a percentage basis, with the government paying one-fifth, say, or one-tenth or some other proportion of the amount raised by public subscription or contributed by municipal and provincial governments. I would ask the minister to take this suggestion into consideration and to give us a decision later.
The minister also spoke of national laboratories. I am glad to know that something is being done in that regard in a very large way when I hope proper provision will be made not only for equipment but for the salaries of research workers. I suggest that a very large sum of money be set aside for research. It is a well known fact that research in medicine in Canada has been starved, and that we spend only a very small proportion per capita of the amount that is spent by other [DOT] countries on research. It is hoped that Canada will take its place among the nations in providing sufficient money to promote research in a much larger way than hitherto. We have had evidence in this house in past sessions of the need for research when one of our members urged that a certain remedy which was found efficacious in a city in the west should be assisted by a federal government money grant. Ultimately I believe some steps were taken in that direction; but if we had had our laboratory here properly equipped

and staffed, it would have been very easy to have this claim of a cure for cancer investigated and the results made known. It is the duty of this government to provide a considerable sum of money for research in cancer, as well as in many other diseases for which cures have not as yet been discovered.
I was glad to hear the minister speak of venereal disease control, and wish to commend the department on the splendid worjf done by Colonel Williams under the former minister. He instituted control throughout Canada, and stimulated the various provinces into similar activity, so we may hope for considerable improvement in the control of this devastating disease.
I should like to speak of another class of cases for whom assistance should be provided in a very large way, that is, the cases to which the hon. member for Lake Centre referred a moment ago, which would include incurable cases of cancer, paralysis and many other diseases. The accommodation for these people is inadequate throughout Canada. In the city of Toronto we have a home which was formerly called the Hospital for Incurables, but the name of which has been changed to the Queen Elizabeth hospital, which was built almost entirely by donations from private individuals. Recently it has extended its accommodation, but still there is a long waiting list of people who never can be accommodated there. I believe the provincial government is doing something in different parts of the province in regard to the hospitalization of chronic cases, and I suggest to the minister that the federal government make a very considerable grant toward the erection of hospitals throughout the country for these incurable cases.
I do not intend to go into all the other matters mentioned by the minister, because I presume we will have an opportunity of discussing them as we go through the estimates item by item. I should like to say just a word on something the minister mentioned, namely, that health insurance has been referred to the provinces. For two sessions I sat as a member of the social security committee considering the question of health insurance. If I may say so, we did a great deal of hard work and received a great deal of information from interested bodies throughout Canada. Our committee received some 116 presentations, and after very careful consideration a draft bill was drawn up called an act respecting health insurance, public health, the conservation of health and the prevention of disease. Of course this legislation could not be put through parliament at that time because it contained a money provision requiring contributions from the provinces; and until the dominion-provin-

cial conference was held and a decision reached as to the amount to be contributed by the federal and provincial governments respectively one can understand that this measure could not be finally dealt with. However, from what the minister said I take it that this bill now is to be superseded by some other arrangement. I should like the minister to clarify this subject, because I had hoped that thisi bill might still be incorporated in any arrangement made with the. provinces. We drafted a model bill which the provinces might use for the purpose of enabling us to have some uniformity in health legislation throughout Canada. If that is not done we will have nine different kinds of health insurance in this country, and I should be very sorry to see that happen because I think it would materially affect the efficiency of any health act. We devised an act which is comprehensive, providing medical, surgical, obstetrical, dental, pharmaceutical, hospita'1 and nursing benefits, and which I believe is an improvement over any health act in operation in any country. Certainly it is an improvement on the act in operation in Great Britain, because thfey provide only general practitioner services whereas in the act proposed here we provide specialist services, and many other benefits not included in the British Act.
Let me repeat that In my opinion it is highly desirable that there should be one national health-insurance act for Canada which should operate in all provinces. Special provisions may be made to meet local conditions in any province; and it should be possible to do this under the terms of this national act. If the provinces desire to make any changes in the act of course that is their prerogative, but I would dislike to see nine different health acts in Canada. I believe it would make for confusion, inefficiency and additional expense. I understand that already certain proposals made to the provinces in regard to' this matter have not met with the approval of all. For instance, a diagnostic service is proposed by Manitoba and preferred by them to the visiting nursing survice. Alberta does not like the nursing service either, and I understand that British Columbia has made counter proposals. So it would appear that there is not likely to be unanimity as far as health insurance legislation is concerned if the provinces individually are allowed to provide whatever health services they wash, and receive grants from the federal government.
I should like to say further, because there is some little conflict of opinion in regard to it, that health insurance is most applicable to low wage earners and persons in the middle 47699-179
income group, and should not be all-inclusive of the higher income groups. If it applied to everyone in the state it would be an invitation to state medicine, which I believe to be entirely undesirable and unacceptable in Canada. You may ask what is meant by state medicine? It has been clearly defined as a medical system by which doctors are hired, paid and controlled by the state-, there being no free choice of doctor by patient. And the doctor-patient relationship is fundamentally important in the treatment of disease. Health insurance, on the other hand, is a plan which permits the establishment of a fund contributed by the employee and the state, on some agreed basis, out of which fund the doctor of the patient's choice is paid for services rendered. It will be seen therefore that there is a vast difference between state medicine and health insurance.
I may say that the medical profession in Canada do not approve of state medicine and would not operate under it; whereas I believe we have every indication from the Canadian Medical Association and other bodies that they are willing to operate under a system of health insurance. I should like to leave further discussion of this question until the various items are before us. I come now to another matter.
Owing to the acute controversy which has arisen as a result of certain opinions expressed in public addresses in the United States and Canada by the deputy minister of health and welfare; I feel in duty bound, as a medical man, to make some observations. On a previous occasion I did not hesitate to defend Doctor Chisholm in this house when he was under attack, but regeret that I cannot conscientiously do so to-day in spite of the support he has received from seven or eight eminent psychologists in messages conveyed to the Prime Minister; for even psychologists may make mistakes.
1 Doctor Chisholm is a psychiatrist and a thoroughly trained psychiatrist at that. After graduation from the faculty of medicine in the university of Toronto he engaged in general practice for a few years. He then spent several years specializing in neurology and completed his training in psychiatry, at the institute of human relations at Yale university. His psychiatric skill has thus been built on an unusual basis of general medicine and special studies in neurology. When he speaks in this particular field his opinion should be heard with the respect due to his studies. It is also possible that the deputy minister has been unduly irritated by certain criticisms directed at the medical services of the armed forces by members of the clergy, both Pro-

Supply-Health and Welfare

testant and Roman Catholic, especially their concern over the methods of prophylaxis employed against the spread of venereal disease.
In that matter there are both medical and moral aspects. The clergy and many others have properly stressed the mdral aspects. Doctor Chisholm may have been almost exclusively concerned with the medical aspects. Even though the Christian position in regard to marriage and self-control is the normative ideal, we have been living in .an abnormal world, and Doctor Chisholm had to deal with that situation. Nevertheless, in my opinion, this does not justify the addresses which he made and which have shocked the Christian conscience of the country, since they seem to suggest that there are no standards of right and wrong at all, that there is no such thing as the "natural law," and that there is no -creative force in the universe that wills good and abhors evil.
He seems to propose the eradication of prohibitions of all definite moral standards. To him at least, so it would seem, all the moral judgments of society are purely relative and based on no eternal and immutable principles such as the natural law presupposes. While not denying Doctor Chisholm the right to hold any views he wishes as a private citizen, views expressed in public addresses gain in importance and influence by virtue of the high government position which he holds. As I said a moment ago, the expressed opinions of the deputy minister have shocked the public conscience of the Canadian people. For while morals go far beyond the civil law, civil law itself has its sanction only as it aims to prevent evil and to promote the good life.
If we regard morals and the laws of God as only the folly of ecclesiastics, may we not be cutting away the ultimate authority of all legislative bodies that pass criminal legislation? Such theories, in my judgment, attack the fundamental basis of law itself. They attack the very basis on which this house legislates in regard to a vast number of subjects. But they do more, for we are a British people and the British seek to be a Christian people. Since Christianity was brought to the shores of Britain and accepted by her kings and rulers we have never enthroned merely the goddess of reason in Westminster Abbey or St. Paul's cathedral. Though there may remain many un-Christian elements in our society, from the beginnings of our recorded history we have held high both the law of God and the law of man. We British are extremely tolerant, and while we are more concerned with how private people'

behave than with what they think, we are fundamentally a Christian people. Our king at his coronation in 1937 took the oath, as did his predecessors, to preserve the sanctities and liberties of the_ church, and sought the blessing of Almighty God on his reign.
In one of the songs extolling Canada, sung by a great many Canadians and heard nightly over some of our broadcasting systems, we express our loyalty to both throne and altar, although certain Canadians do not seem particularly to care for the reference to the throne while other Canadians are annoyed at the references to the altar. A minister of the crown or even his deputy will not, however, cast aspersions on either throne or altar with impunity.
These are my public judgments, but privately, and even as a member of the medical profession, I take the same position. As a believer in God,I believe in the moral law and accept the Christian revelation. It is increasingly clear to all social students to-day that the whole of civilization stands on the brink of an abyss. Scientists do not hesitate to express their fears that our world may even be wiped out. Scientists who in the past have seemed most neutral are becoming the champions of the moral law. On every hand voices are heard demanding a return to spiritual values, even though the traditional values may need to have some of their dross and barnacles removed. But in my judgment this is no time in the history of the world to do or to say anything that challenges the moral foundations of life.

My original reason for rising was to talk about the Connaught laboratories in the city of Toronto. I wish to pay a tribute to three institutions which have had to do with what I have to say, namely, the university of Toronto, the Canadian Red Cross, and the National Research Council. In addition to that I wish to pay tribute to Professor C. H. Best, of the university of Toronto. The best way I can pay tribute to him and the institution is by relating the facts. In September, 1939, at the Connaught laboratories in the university of Toronto, a project for the preparation of dried blood serum, used to treat conditions of secondary shock or bums, was commenced. Most hon. members know that from ten to fifteen per cent of the wounded require some form of transfusion. It may be interesting to note that from June 6 to September the British army used 28,709 pints of dried plasma.
To begin with, the problems were many. First, preliminary studies were made as to the chemical and clinical aspects of plasma. Then it had to be dried so as to make sure that there was no change in the physical or chemical properties of the material. Then there was the further problem of storing the material without its losing its value. As the value of the work was appreciated, naturally the work increased. There was the need of accommodation and funds. Then the federal government took a hand and entered into an agreement with the Connaught laboratories and the Canadian Red Cross on January 1, 1941, whereby the federal government paid for the operation and maintenance costs, the laboratories paid for the management, administration and necessary overhead, and the Red Cross provided the supplies of normal human blood.

It is interesting to note that when Professor Best first started he obtained what blood he could from his own staff, the staff of the school of hygiene and the students of the university of Toronto. His staff consisted of three people, and his accommodation was one laboratory bench, one table, ^nd one bed. As the work increased, the Toronto blood donor clinic was opened by the Red Cross; and as hon. members know some 662 clinics were later opened across this country. I think it. is well to record here the names of the men and women who originally helped Professor Best, because they are names to remember. They were: Doctor D. Y. Solandt, Doctor Jessie Ridout, Doctor R. R. Haist, Doctor L. Chute, Doctor E. Fidler and Mr. Campbell Cowan. They did the preliminary and pioneer work, and the process used in preparation of dried serum even now is a direct result, modified in the light of experience, of their work.
Thus, directly or indirectly, serum prepared, at the university of Toronto from blood collected from volunteer donors has been used by our troops of the three services fromi Alaska to the Mediterranean. There never was a shortage. They worked seven days a week and twenty-four hours a day; but it was the Red Cross which really drew the blood. In 1944 they had 868,000 donations in 662 clinics. The staff was almost entirely voluntary; it consisted of physicians, nurses, housewives, and people right across Canada. In addition to that, the Red Cross established laboratories in Halifax, Fredericton, Winnipeg, Saskatoon, Edmonton and Vancouver for the preliminary preparation of serum in cooperation with the universities in those places. Then the laboratories forwarded the partly processed serum to Toronto for the completion of the process of drying.
The university of Toronto shipped over 400,000 bottles of dried blood to the Canadian and allied, forces; the Red Cross collected altogether over two and a half million donations, and the Canadian government spent one and a half million dollars. Now I get down to the real crux of the situation. The Connaught laboratories spent $90,000 for direction and overhead, and $54,000 for alteration, of the building, a total of $144,000. At the present time the Canadian government has ire the Connaught laboratories $100,000 ini equipment and $42,000 in unexpended supplies, a total of $142,000. The committee has the two figures. speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to
Provide by amendment to the Export Credits nsurance Act that the aggregate -amount of 
loans made and outstanding at any -time and the value of securities purchased or acquired and held at any one time under section twenty-two of the said Act shall be increased from $100,000,000 to $750,000,000.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair perhaps an explanation would be desirable and- then if any questions arise out of the explanation they can be dealt with in committee.
The house will recall that the Export Credits Insurance Act was passed at the session of 1944. There were two parts to that act. Part I established a corporation to engage in the insurance of commercial export credits. This corporation is responsible to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Part II permitted- the governor in council to authorize the Minister of Finance to enter into agreements with foreign governments or their agencies to provide them with credits, or to guarantee credits provided to them by others in Canada "for the purpose- of facilitating and developing trade between Canada and- any other country.'r
The purpose of the proposed legislation is to increase the amount which the government may lend to other governments or their agencies under part II of the Export Credits Insurance Act from $100,000,000 to $750,000,000. No alteration is proposed in the amount ,of the guarantees which the government may give, that is, $200,000,000, or in the amount of business which the insurance corporation is authorized to do.
The government has decided not to introduce amendments to part I of the act at this session, because to do so would unduly crowd the legislative programme. Amendments to part I will be proposed at the next session. Perhaps there will be other amendments to part II, but the main- amendments to be proposed at the next session I expect will be to part I. These will include the amendments which were made by order in council last summer prior to the assembling of parliament, when it was necessary to make certain detailed amendments in order to permit the business of export insurance to begin on the most effective basis. The order in council relating to this matter was tabled some months ago. Possibly there will be an opportunity when discussing these amendments for questions in this regard to be answered, but that is a matter for my colleague, the Minister of Trade and, -Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon).
The purpose of the proposed amendment is to give the government sufficient authority to make loans to allied governments in the next year or two to enable them to purchase supplies from Canada required by them during the period of reconstruction to repair the

Export Credits Insurance
damage caused to their countries during the war and reestablish their export trade and normal financial machinery. It is not the purpose of this amendment to provide funds for making loans to the United Kingdom or the sterling area generally. Discussions are proceeding at the present time in Washington regarding credits or a credit from the United States to the United Kingdom, and we expect that Canada will a little later be providing a large credit for the United Kingdom. We hope and expect that as a result of this credit to the United Kingdpm she will not need to follow a programme of such rigid austerity as she is following at this moment and will be able to continue to take from Canada in the next year or two most of the products which our economy has been organized to supply to her in the past.

speechtext: That will be quite apart from this resolution?

subtopic: INCREASE IN AMOUNT OF LOANS AND VALUE OF SECURITIES HELD UNDER SECTION 22
speechtext:
Yes. We have not as yet discussed the matter with the United Kingdom and do not expect to do so until they have concluded discussions with the United States. We expect to come back to parliament next session for additional legislative authority to make large credits available to the United Kingdom in one form or another. I therefore do not propose to enter at this time into a discussion of the term's and conditions of credits to the United Kingdom or on the general United Kingdom and sterling area financial and trade situation.
The funds which are to be provided under the legislation which will follow this resolution are to enable us to make loans to allied countries other than the United Kingdom. More specifically, and in accordance with the details which I shall supply, we would propose to use the bulk of this money for loans to our allies in western Europe, the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, China and the Netherlands East Indies. The government has already told the government of France that if parliament grants the necessary authority we will lend France Canadian dollars to a total of $242,500,000 to make purchases in Canada this year and next year. We have also given similar undertakings to lend the Netherlands' $60,000,000 in addition to the $25,000,000 we have already lent that government; to lend Norway $17,000,000 in addition to the $13,000,000 we have already made available to the Norwegian government; and to lend the Bank for the Netherlands Indies, as agent for the government of the Netherlands Indies, a further $50,000,000 in addition to the $15,000,000 already made available.
In the case of Belgium we have agreed to increase the $25,000,000 we have made available to her government by an amount still to be determined after further consideration of her requirements in Canada and the means of financing them. The amount and terms of a loan to the government of China are at present under discussion with representatives of that government, but we have indicated our willingness to lend an amount to China to enable her to finance part of her post-war requirements in Canada. We are also negotiating with the U.S.S.R., which is interested in obtaining loans from Canada to purchase some supplies originally requested as Mutual Aid, the production of which has been under way, as well as credits to buy ether exports for which will be' placed with the U.S.S.R. after agreements upon the credits. As yet no amount for a credit to U.S.S.R., apart from the small one of $3,000,000 already reported to the house, has been decided upon pending further discussion about terms, but I feel that in forecasting our requirements we should make liberal provision for the needs in Canada of the U.S.S.R.
In addition we have had inquiries from several other allied countries, and it may be that some countries in the sterling area, India, for example, may wish to get credits from us quite apart from any large credit provided to the United Kingdom. We have not yet reached the stage of negotiating with any other countries than those I have mentioned, but we feel that we should have a modest margin to meet new situations.
The basis, then, of the figure of $650,000,000 in addition to the present $100,000,000, is to provide the specific amounts which I have just mentioned-to France, the Netherlands, the Netherlands Indies and Norway-to enable us to conclude negotiations and provide reasonable amounts to Belgium, China and the U.S.S.R., and to leave us some margin for other requirements which may develop in the future.
The house may wish to know something about the major policies being followed in determining these loans. In the first place we are recognizing Canada's interest in the economic reconstruction of the allied countries. Canada has an immediate interest in reviving and developing our export trade during the reconstruction period, and the orders that have been placed by these countries have already been of great value. The credits have enabled our European allies particularly to place large orders with us not only for food and materials but for manufactures, railway equipment, ships and so on.

Mr. Speaker, I have only one word to say before you leave the' chair. I am sure hon. members must be in entire accord with the object behind this measure, because the helping of various nations of the world has become the task of countries like Canada, the United States and others which are in a prosperous condition. But when I listened' to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) this afternoon I was greatly disappointed to hear him say that no concessions were to be asked from these nations when loans were negotiated. What I have in mind is this: It was indicated by the minister -at least the understanding was implicit- that in the state of world affairs as we have it to-day, one of the conditions of the making of loans to countries needing them would be the breaking or tearing down of tariff walls and barriers. Let us consider France for a moment. I do not know what the conditions are to-day, but I know that before the war, from 1930 on, it was almost impossible for Canada to ship

wheat to' France, owing to the high tariff barriers which had been erected. If one looks over the subsidies paid in France, Italy and Germany from 1930 to 1939, he will readily see that the subsidies paid for wheat alone in those three countries would have bought more wheat from Canada, and have landed it in those countries, than the subsidies amounted to.
There may be those in the house who differ from me when I say that if there was one thing more than anything else which brought on the war it was the fact that the people in one country, because of high tariff walls, could not have the benefit of goods from another country. Before the war, tariff walls were built around each country, and brought poverty in those countries and some distress in this one. Surely the time has come when we should say to those countries who built high tariff walls, "We will help you; we realize you need this money and food; but for the benefit of your own people we want you right now to take down those tariff walls and let Canadian wheat and other goods from this country enter without tariff." If we are to do anything to improve the living conditions of people in other lands, this is one of the limitations we should impose. I was disappointed when the minister told us that such matters were only incidental to the discussion. I should like to know when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) are going to deal with these things and say, "We are demanding that you take down tariff walls to help your own people, and help us too." It seems to me there is no difficulty at all in connection with finance. The government is able to give these countries goods, but how is it that when questions in connection with old age pensions are brought up, the question of where to find the money is always raised? Surely what is possible for one is possible for another.
I rose chiefly to speak about tariff walls, and restrictions against our goods entering other countries. Now is the time to bring down those tariffs and carry out the terms of the
Atlantic charter. There are many people on the North American continent who think that living conditions here are normal. I say that our living conditions are abnormal and the condition of people in other countries is just miserable. Mr. Speaker, since this resolution appeared on the order paper I believe some publicity has been given to it and I have been reflecting upon the subject. I have been trying to think my way through the subject of this resolution to the end' that I could understand it. The peculiar thing is that when our own people were in need of goods in days *gone by, the government, which was the same government that exists to-day, could not find it possible to advance money to our own people so that they would be able to buy their own goods. I cannot quite see how that ties up.
Thinking of pictures, this is the thought that has gone through my mind. Here is a man in business, perhaps a grocery business- people need food-with a clothing department -people need clothes. He stands behind his counter and would like to sell his goods. People come into his place of business and look around at the goods on his shelves. Upon making inquiries he finds that the people want to buy his goods but they have no money. So a bright idea comes to him. He opens his till and he says to his customers, "I see the only reason you are not buying my goods is that yoil have no money." He takes money from his till and gives it to the people in his .^tore and they immediately begin to buy his .-goods. I do not know whether that is a good policy, but I am quite certain if any business man in Canada did that people would consider lie was crazy. I have never known anybody "ito do it yet, but it seems to me that that is what we are doing with this legislation. If it is not, I should like the minister to explain why 'it is not.
Mr. ILSLEY; Because it is not a gift.
Mr. HANSELiL: I cannot see why we do not just give them the goods and say, "There is a debt standing against you and we hope you

speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member for New Westminster said that if we could raise $750 million for export credits we ought to be able to raise the money just as easily for social services. I suppose the raising of the money is'just as easy in one case as in the other, but the two transactions are different. In the case of payment for social services, that money is paid out and is not recovered. As far as the taxpayers as a whole are concerned, they' get nothing back. On the other hand these are loans, represented by assets, and we hope they will be recovered. We expect that in large measure they will be recovered, because most of these countries are excellent credit risks. As I stated, we must take some risk; any country making loans to other countries takes a risk, the world being in the condition it is in to-day, but as far as the people of Canada as a whole are concerned they are entitled to a return and it is expected that they will get a return in future ye^rs for what they send out of the country now. So that to	mind-and I hope it is
not impaired by concentration on financial considerations-a loan is different from a gift even when one is making the gift to some of the people in one's own country.
Then the hon. member for New Westminster safd that we should have seized the opportunity to tie up these countries in regard to tariffs, to get them to agree to keep their tariffs down, or not to raise them, or something of that kind. Well, in the case of France, which he mentioned, we did get them to insert a clause providing for most favoured nation treatment, and that is as far as we have gone. If you go much further than that you have to embark upon protracted trade negotiations, and of course they would be entitled to obtain similar assurances from.us with reference to our tariff. Negotiations of that type take a-long time. You can go only so far in tying up two matters which are only partly related. These transactions on their face get markets for our goods, apart altogether from the tariffs of these other countries. They effect the purpose, for the time being at any rate, of getting markets for our goods. I do not think the United States, in dealing with these countries through their export-import bank, have undertaken to connect them with commercial negotiations. We considered that, and we decided it was impracticable. The negotiations would be almost endless if we did that. These other countries might very well say, "That is all right, but you must go over your tariff and tell us what you are going to do with it.'' Certainly we could not have concluded such negotiations at all rapidly, and I doubt the [Mr. Ilsley.l
practicability of doing it. The one is a loan transaction by which we get a market for our production. The other is something else again, which of course we shall have to undertake pretty soon. It is very easy to say, "You are in the driver's seat. You can snap your whip and say they must do this or that with their tariffs for the next twenty-five or thirty years or they do not get their money." I am not now referring to wheat, I am referring to other commodities. The Canadian export board was formed to carry out the procurement of civilian type goods, recognizing that as foreign countries begin to buy these goods rather than to receive them under mutual aid, the same rigorous buying policy that was necessarily and properly followed by the Department of Munitions and Supply -might not now be practicable. This policy recognizes that the Canadian export board exists primarily for the benefit of Canadian producers in assisting them to obtain and develop markets for their product and as such is filling an essentially different function from that of the wartime procurement agency primarily occupied in buying -munitions of war with the money of the taxpayers.

That it is expedient to present a measure to authorize the Minister of Finance, with the_ approval of the governor in council to enter into an agreement with the province of Alberta to pay the province increased amounts by way of compensation and subsidy over the amounts agreed to be so paid under an agreement entered into with the province, dated March 30, 1942.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

That meant paying them $600,000 a year for 1937, 1938, 1939 and 1940, and paying them an amount I have not before me at the moment for the years following, 1941, 1942, 1943 and on up to the end of the tax agreement, which they would have been entitled to under the offer we made if they had been paying the full interest on their bonds. Now that their bonds fall due they can refund at much lower rates of interest than they would be able to if they did not do this, so that apart from the principle of the thing it is good business for the province.

I did not want to interject anything into this debate, but it seems to me that the hon. member for Cariboo is attempting a little bit of propaganda in this whole business. As a matter of fact, in all our negotiations there was one thing uppermost in our minds, from the time I started these negotiations six. years ago, and it was this. We feel that it was our obligation to the holders of Alberta bonds to see that the pricb of those bonds rose to or near par at the earliest possible date. That was our obligation, and we have taken whatever action was required to bring the market value back so that the holders of bonds might dispose of them and not take a severe loss.
Actually, this resolution, or the bill that may follow, is not for the purpose of making good the total of the unpaid interest on those bonds, and it is not a question of what the people of Alberta have saved or what they are saving. It is a question of carrying through an agreement between the federal government and the government of Alberta to make good a payment that would have been given to the province of Alberta since 1941 had that province selected the debt service option under the tax transfer agreement. If anyone wishes to make political capital of it this is rather a poor place to do so.
I compliment, the minister on a good job done. My only regret is that it was not done years ago.' It could have been accomplished had we got around the table a little more amicably and with a little more spirit of understanding. I am sure it could have been done. I wish to compliment the minister on having taken a fair attitude toward the whole matter and upon helping us to get the thing cleared away, because it has meant a great
Alberta Tax Agreement

deal not only to the people of Alberta and the government of that province but to the whole of Canada. I have felt that for some years.
I wish to thank my colleague for the kindly things he said about me. He did not have to say1 them because I have taken it in the line of my duty. I felt it was my responsibility.

I simply rise to say that it hardly becomes the leader of the Social Credit group to take umbrage at anyone for raising a political point, because his own group is adept at that kind of thing. My colleague the hon. member for Cariboo asked a very proper question. Here the government of Canada has undertaken to pay certain sums of money to a provincial government, and he wanted to have it clear as to the particular reason for the Dominion of Canada paying these sums. I think he is entitled to an answer.

There is one thing else that ought to be said. When Premier Aberhart led the social credit movement to the successful victory of 1935, >
it was never his intention, nor was it the intention of the social credit movement, that anyone should lose as a result of Alberta's determined effort to obtain some sort of justice in the matter of financial arrangements. It ought to foe known, and for the sake of those who were not in the house at the time I am going to say, that the province of Alberta was owing a great deal of money at an interest rate which in the light of conditions was fantastic. Imagine owing millions of dollars at an interest rate of six and a half per cent! It was utterly impossible for that province to obtain an adjustment with regard to that interest rate without exactly the measures which they did take under Premier Aberhart.
It is due to Premier Aberhart, seeing that he has gone beyond the veil, that it be stated here that the very first thing he did after he became premier of Alberta was to come east with the objeqt of seeing the financial authorities of Canada at that time in order to obtain a system of refunding Alberta's debt. Had the president of the Bank of Canada and other financial authorities in the dominion had the vision-and it is impossible now to see why they did not have it-they would have sat round the council table with Premier Aberhart and allowed him to refund that great debt of Alberta at a lower interest rate, and all the unhappiness which has resulted from Alberta's defaulting would have been avoided. I feel it is only fair that this be said with respect to the late .Premier Aberhart. 
I look upon him as one of the greatest statesmen in the Dominion of Canada since confederation. Had't not been for the determined stand which that man took, with the province of Alberta behind him, we would not even yet be thinking in terms of interest rates as reasonable, as we now know them. Very shortly after the determined stand that Alberta took, we found a tendency toward lower interest rates in Ontario and in other parts of the dominion. Interest rates should be even lower than they are to-day.
