speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in connection tvith this item I think it would be well if I were to make a statement to the committee with regard to Abasand Oils Limited. The Minister of Munitions and Supply in 1942 recommended that the bituminous sand of northern Alberta should come under immediate and detailed examination, in order to determine whether large oil production could be obtained from it. At that time all possible sources of Canadian production were being investigated with a view to offsetting the loss of oil supplies through the sinking of many oil-tankers by enemy action.
On April 14, 1943, the minister reported progress made, outlining the problem still to be solved, and stated that the government had arranged to take title to the plant of Abasand Oils Limited near Fort McMurray as the best method of implementing a recommendation of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Com-

Supply-Mines and Resources
pany of Canada which had earned on an investigation for the government the previous year.
The arrangement was that the government did not pay compensation to the Aba-sand company for the plant and equipment but was to provide funds to the company for rehabilitating the plant and for carrying out pilot plant operations on mining and treatment of the sand.
The company for its part accepted responsibility for reconstructing of the plant, developing processes for the mining and treatment of the bituminous sands, and obtaining cost data for the various operations.
On May 25, 1944, the then minister of mines and resources reviewed in the House of Commons the progress made under the agreement with Abasand Oils Limited and pointed out the difficulties that had arisen in connection with construction, owing to the scarcity of materials and of satisfactory labour. He indicated that the separation plant was expected to be in operation during the summer, and that operation of the refinery would follow a few months later.
In June, 1944, the separation plant was sufficiently completed for test runs, but operations were on an intermittent or limited basis for several months owing to the need for further separation and refinery equipment and completion of the power house as well as to lack of storage space for production. In December, 1944, the refinery made an initial run and from then on operations were continued on a larger scale. The various handicaps itemized above had been almost entirely overcome by June 16, 1945, when unfortunately, the separation plant, workshops and warehouse were destroyed by fire. It is possible, however, as a result of operations up to that time to arrive at tentative conclusions with regard to the project.
Mining. Commercial utilization of the bituminous sands unquestionably involves year-round operation. Work carried out under the Abasand agreement has demonstrated that mining presents no serious difficulty; in the summer a powerful shovel can excavate the sands without blasting, and in the winter, provided that a reasonably large tonnage were continuously handled, only a' relatively thin surface layer of frozen material would require blasting.
Separation. Operation of theTMcClave hot-water process as it was carried out in the separation plant revealed several weaknesses. The amount of heat required to maintain the pulp at a temperature of 175 degrees Fahrenheit was costly, since thirty per cent to forty per cent of the products recovered from the bitumen were required for heating and power.
Further, the distillation of a small amount of the lighter fractions of the bitumen created unhealthy working conditions in the separation plant.	[DOT]
A new method of recovering the bitumen from the sand was therefore developed which appears to have definite advantages over the hot-water process inasmuch as separation is carried out at a temperature of approximately 75 degrees Fahrenheit. Results of operation on the basis of treatment of about 100 tons a day over a period of three months, as reported by the Abasand management, indicated lower costs, higher yields of bitumen, and greater recovery of the diluent oil used in the process. An enlarged unit of 600-ton capacity was being installed to verify these results when the separation plant was destroyed by fire.
Refinery. Operation of the refinery was limited by the comparatively small output of the separation plant. Test runs indicated that the refinery had a capacity of 1,300 barrels of diluted crude, equal to about 600 barrels of bitumen, a day. It is designed for thermal cracking of the bitumen, after recovery of the diluent used in the separation process, yielding a small amount of gasoline, some diesel oil, residual fuel oil, and asphalt. Production of higher grade products from, the bitumen demands a much more elaborate and more costly refining process, involving both thermal and catalytic cracking, isomerization and alkylation units, or, alternatively, hydrogenation.
Cost estimates. While the government has not yet received a final report from the company of the results obtained up to the time of the fire, from data collected in the intermittent operations of the plant, certain deductions and estimates have been made by the Abasand management on the cost of obtaining a barrel of bitumen from sands containing sixteen per cent bitumen, and on the cost of obtaining petroleum products from it on the basis of a production of 500 barrels of bitumen a day.

Products derived from the crude are assumed to be. gasoline, 7 per cent; make-up diluent, 6 per cent; diesel oil, 10 per cent; fuel oil, 19-7 ]jer cent; asphalt, 56* 3 per cent; gas and loss, one per cent. The gasoline is not of the best grade as it contains two per cent of sulphur, removal of which would lead to a considerable reduction in yield and increased cost of production. The make-up diluent is delivered to the separation plant and is therefore saleable to the operation. The diesel oil is of reasonably good quality and is comparable to grades now being used commercially. The fuel oil is too heavy for domestic heating units but is suitable for central heating plant installations. The asphalt is of good quality but would require further processing for production of asphalts to specification.
The cost of producing jbilumen as feed stock for complete refining or hydrogenation has been estimated, on the basis of 500 barrels a day throughout at approximately 11.60 a barrel.
Marketing. The estimated total revenue from the -sale in Edmonton of such products as can be made by the refinery now installed at the Abasand plant has been estimated as equivalent to $2.85 a barrel of bitumen, showing an apparent return of $0.34 over and above the operating costs of the plant. However, the cost of rail transportation to Edmonton under current classifications and' rates has been calculated as equivalent to $1.78 a barrel, which transportation would result in a marketing loss of $1.44 a barrel of bitumen processed.
Since freight rates are large factors in marketing costs, a study was made in order, to estimate the effect of different rates on the revenue obtainable. Transportation costs were recalculated using alternative rates for heavy fuel oil and for asphalt. When a rate of 45 cents .per hundredweight was used for both heavy fuel oil and asphalt, the freight charges were reduced from $1.78 a barrel to $1.61, and when a rate of 26 cents was used, they were reduced still further to $1.11 a barrel. However, the net revenue still failed to equal operating costs by $1.27 and $0.77, respectively, per barrel of bitumen processed.
Therefore it does not appear to be possible to recover the operating costs of processing bitumen by marketing the products at Edmonton under existing freight rates when the operating cost is $2.51 per barrel of bitumen processed.
It is possible that development of the mining industry in the Northwest Territories within the comparatively near future would expand the market for petroleum products very

considerably. If development occurred around lake Athabaska the capacity of the McMurray-Waterways area to utilize pertoleum products would be correspondingly enlarged. In this connection the potential market at Yellowknife was investigated but the results were disappointing. Heavy fuel oil, such as could be produced at Abasand by combining the asphalt, fuel oil and diesel fuel oil fractions of the bitumen, sells at $0.19 a gallon laid down at Yellowknife, from Norman Wells; freight alone on the Abasand product from Waterways would amount to $0.16 a gallon, leaving a net return of approximately $0.03 a gallon to the company. This would make a total net revenue to the company of about $1.62 per barrel of bitumen processed.
With the decline in production of well petroleum in Alberta, imports of crude oil into the western provinces have increased. In the first seven months of 1945 these imports totalled 2,427,770 barrels, and in the same period a substantial subsidy was paid by the government in order to avoid the necessity of permitting increased prices for petroleum products in Canada. If it is found to be expedient to discontinue payment of the subsidy, then increased prices for crude oil and for petroleum products generally may be expected. If the price of crude increased by $0.70 a barrel, then a corresponding increase totalling two cents per gallon of products will follow. However, this increase will not likely be applied equally to all products, and it is practically certain that the lighter products such as gasoline and light fuel oils, which are in greater demand, will absorb practically all the increased cost. Therefore, it is believed that the competitive price of heavy fuel oil and asphalt will not likely be increased more than one cent a gallon for such increase of $0.70 a barrel in the price of crude oil. Such an increase would result in the net revenues of the company being increased by approximately $0.50 a barrel of bitumen.
_ The government entered into the present investigation of Athabaska bituminous sands under the stress of a war-time emergency and many factors combined to delay the completion of the programme. The objective was to obtain reliable data concerning treatment of the sand and the cost of extracting bitumen from it. A pilot plant of approximately 500 barrels a day capacity was used for the purpose, but it was not expected to be a revenue producing operation. Some results have been obtained which permit tentative conclusions to be drawn regarding the cost of obtaining petroleum products from the bituminous sands, but they are not as conclusive as is

Supply-Mines and Resources
desired. Under present conditions the cost would appear to approximate 81.60 per barrel of crude bitumen and $2.50 per barrel of refinery products therefrom. These figures, however, require to be verified' by steady operation of the plant before they could be accepted with complete assurance and before they could be used as basic cost figures for calculations under changed conditions that will arise inevitably in the future. It should be emphasized that the Abasand plant is a pilot plant for investigational work; it is not a commercial production plant, and the revenue obtained as a result of its operation was not expected to' exceed the cost by an amount sufficient to make it an economic operation unless a profitable market develops. Information as to this revenue is required for determining whether or not profitable operation of large-scale commercial plants is possible.
The expenditures made by the Abasand company in carrying out the investigation have clearly shown that the sands can be mined without any serious obstacles even under winter conditions, and with the more powerful equipment that would be used in large scale operations no mining difficulties should be encountered. Again, the investigation has resulted in the development of a new method of separating the bitumen from the sand. This process appears to have definite advantages over the hot-water process formerly used, indicating lower costs, increased recoveries of bitumen from the sands and lower loss of the diluent used in the process. It has been shown also that for high recovery of bitumen and low diluent loss, the feed to the separation plant should consist of freshly mined unoxidized sand.
A study of the markets for the products of the present plant show-s that under prevailing conditions as to freight rates these products cannot be sold at a profit where consumption exists, and that the only profitable market would be within a radius of a few hundred miles of the plant where consumption at present is limited to a fraction of the plant's productive capacity. Mining and natural resources developments in the lake Athabaska area and in the vicinity of Waterways might make the operation of such a plant profitable. A much more favourable freight rate and an increased selling price for asphalt would be required before the plant output could compete with asphalt produced from present refineries in the western provinces.
It is appreciated that the cost of producing bitumen could likely be considerably reduced if a large commercial plant were constructed. It is evident, however, that there would not
be a market for Lae quantities of asphalt produced from the large plant. Therefore it would appear that the commercial utilization depends not only on securing much lower costs for mining and separating, the sands, but upon processing the extracted bitumen so as to produce a large proportion of the high price petroleum products. This can be done practicably only in a large-scale refinery of the order of 10,000 barrels a day capacity, embodying thermal and catalytic cracking, isomerization and alkylation'units, or alternatively by hydrogenation. The investigation carried out by Universal Oil Product^ of Chicago into full cracking process indicated that the required products cannot be obtained profitably at the present time. Their estimate of the cost of a 5,000 barrel a day refinery in Canadian funds was $12,000,000. No reliable information is available as to the economics or as to the cost of building a commercial plant. From the information available it is not likely that a 10,000 barrel a day plant could be constructed for less than $25,000,000. When the cost of the same size separation plant, probably $10,000,000, is included it will be observed that substantial capital expenditures are necessary.
It will also be appreciated that the commercial utilization of the sands depends as well upon the costs of getting the products to the available markets. The present freight rate of $1.78 per barrel of products makes it impossible to compete with Turner valley crude oil. However, these costs would be substantially reduced if a pipeline were constructed to provide an outlet for the products of'a large commercial plant.

I listened with interest to what the minister said, and I should like to point out that the McClave system was in operation in that plant in 1944. In May, 1945, a supposedly new and improved system was put in operation, and the fire occurred on June 16, I believe. We are led to believe that in that short space of time this supposedly new and improved system, the Geco system, demonstrated its superiority.

I have a comparison of the operations when we experimented with the
McClave process and the Geco process. The comparative operations were from January 20 to February 4 and from February 21 to March 9; from March 10 to March 26; from April 24 to May 22; and from April 10 to April 12. There is another report which I received in October on the McClave and Geco operating efficiency. They were experimenting and testing as to the efficacy of either system, and one paragraph of the report states that in so far as is known the Geco flotation process is the simplest yet devised for the separation of bitumen from sand. Low temperatures are used. The high temperatures of other processes are offset by the rubbing action of sand particles in the agitation section of the Geco cells. It has been found that most of the middlings returned by the settlers were composed of sand particles from which the oil had not been removed. As the sand particles are under high heat during both separation and settling for many hours, it cannot be expected that the same treatment repeated will result in any further separation. On the other hand, middlings produced by the Geco process are composed of sand particles covered with oi! which have mechanically come with the froth. The additional rubbing in the Geco middling cells cleans off the last of the oil.

The McClave is as simple as anything could be. What could be more simple than water heated to 180 degrees and the agitation of the McClave quiet flotation tank in which sand goes to the bottom, oil comes to the top and then is taken off the same as is done in gold mining. I understood the minister to say that the Geco system operated at about 75 degrees. It- appears to me that the hotter you have the water, the easier it will work because that is all that is required to disintegrate the sand. I doubt very much if water heated to 75 degrees will disintegrate the sand as rapidly as water heated to 180 degrees. The McClave system is in operation in the plants in the United States, and I am sure, if there is any other system better than the McClave system, they would be glad to know about it. The McClave system I am told is used in Brazil in working their large deposits. I am sure they would be glad to know that the government working at Fort McMurray and limiting itself to a few tests carried on almost before the plant was completed had decided that some new system is better.
It is not for me to say that the Geco system is not a good one. I hope it is a good system. I am going to advise the minister to make inquiries and get in touch with the best available men. I understand that next week there will be passing through Ottawa a man who is

expert in the taking of oil from sands. If I happen to see him I am going to send him to the minister's office. I did not know that this matter was coming up to-night and I was not prepared to talk on it. However, I have some recollections of my past investigations and I was able to say something.
I remember when this came up in the house previously and the matter of hydrogenation was discussed. That is a simple system. Hydrogenation is simply the use of a catalyst to crack, to break up the molecules. It is applied to many different things. The Germans had it down to perfection and I suggested that we send someone to Germany to try to get one of the plants they had. If the minister is going to come into the house to ask for a vote of $750,000 to build a hydrogenation plant here, he should make a full investigation. I am going to send to the best engineers I can get in touch with in the United States, men who are qualified!, to see whether we are to have the proper type of hydrogenation plant.
We have good men here; I met some of them at the plant on Booth street. Some of these men could be sent to Germany, and perhaps the department has already done so; if so, they should have reports as to whether it would be profitable for us to bring over a German hydrogenation plant. I will support any vote to make use of these sands.
When rwe get to the vote I propose to discuss that matter.

That is about all I have to say. We were told in 1943-44 by the Minister of Munitions and Supply that by the fall of 1943-44 I believe this country would recover from those sands with the plant checked up by Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company enough bitumen to sell to the United States government for the Alaska highway to pay for our investment. I should like to know why that was not carried out and why we went through all this other business to try to get oil.

government, in deciding whether or not to continue with these operations at Abasand and therefore spending money there, are familiar with the results which have been achieved by the drilling of over one hundred holes in that area by the Imperial Oil Company. May I say to my hon. friends to my left that I am very proud that the .provincial government of Alberta have abandoned faith in what the dominion government are doing and are trying on their own to find out what those sands contain. This may be said in all truth, that in the two years and more in which this government has been spending its money there it has found out exactly nothing; we are not a bit farther advanced than when we started. It does seem to me that the government, without being too proud, might consult other people who have done a bit of work there and whose information might help to determine government policy. Apparently the distinguished gentlemen whom the minister is now consulting have heard nothing of what I am telling them, but I know for a fact that over a hundred holes were drilled by the Imperial Oil Company in that area and they got a lot of information. Their difficulty is that you find there the oil-bearing sand and then a strata of mud. That is not the technical name for it, but it is mud. They are not far up the river from where the government was doing its work, and I am merely asking whether the government officials, being wise gentlemen, have taken into consideration the facets discovered by the Imperial Oil Company.

I am informed of the drilling that has been done by the Imperial Oil Company. They did quite a large amount of drilling, but the department has done very much more drilling. Any information that the Imperial Oil have with regard to their drilling is known to our officers. As a matter of fact, $200,000 has been spent by us in drilling alone.

I do not pretend to be an authority, but I am sure that Imperial Oil Company, no matter what the amount of money spent, have drilled a great many more holes than the government ever thought of doing. I believe that to be the simple fact because that is all they were
doing-just drilling these holes. I know what their difficulty was about six months ago. It was to determine whether in view of the unproductive sand that lies between the various oil-bearing strata which they struck admitted of commercially feasible operations. I am sorry even to seem to disagree with the minister. I am not saying that he is wrong, but I am much inclined to think there is some error in the information which he has innocently just given to the committee.
I am informed that the facts are as I have stated them. We spent about $200,000 in drilling this year and have proved up 258,000,000 tons of sand in one area.

It is very easy to say one has proven 258,000,000 tons, but have they found it in depth, without being interlarded with unproductive stuff, which means a great deal of course in the cost of operation? I am quite sure that the minister means to be correct, but did he say that they have proven 258,000,000 tons which are commercially feasible? That is the problem we have there. We know there is plenty of oil; there is no question about that. We know, for example, that there is plenty of gold in the world: you have it in the sea, you have it everywhere, but can you get it out commercially? Is the minister's statement to this committee this, that in this year they have proven 258,000,000 tons of commercially feasible oil sand in that area? I should be very much interested to know.

The information I have given is that we have spent this $200,000 and have proved up 258,000,000 tons of sand averaging about 12 per cent. But the problem is as to its commercial value after it is processed; and that is the burden of the statement which I made in connection with the report on the Abasand company.

Just a word before this item passes. I do not intend to spend much time discussing this problem, because I have discussed it at great length on many other occasions.
Away back about 1912, I think, if I recall the history of it aright, the federal government first took a hand in investigating the feasibility of producing oil from the tar sands of Athabaska. Some $25,000 was spent at first in sending some of this tar sand over to England and having it analysed. The information which the federal government then got was negative. Since that time they have spent a good deal more money, the minister said about $200,000, and they have got to exactly the same place where they got about 1912; that is they have got nowhere.

As I said in the house a year ago, I was of the opinion that the federal government would not get very far in their experimentation with the Athabaska tar sand because, as my opinion was then and as it is now, they never took it seriously. That was a mistake. We should have gone ahead to develop it on a commercial basis. A year ago the urgency was great; the shortage of gasoline was extreme, and this country was in danger of defeat for lack of fuel oil. Yet this federal government did not see fit to go ahead and put forth the efforts which should have been put forth in developing the tar sands there. If an emergency such as the world war could not move them I am quite sure that a few speeches now will not move them.
The report which the minister has just given us is nothing more than I had expected. I am in hopes, though, that the provincial government will go ahead with their plans-of course they cannot do so on nearly the scale which is possible to the federal government- and will get somewhere. When I was in Edifionton last fall the provincial minister of public works, who wras in charge of this operation, gave me the assurance that they were progressing very satisfactorily. It was his opinion then that the federal government had by their method sabotaged the Athabaska tar sands. That statement, which he made over a year ago, I read into Hansard when I was speaking here on the subject. It seems that the federal government are endeavouring to wash their hands of the whole thing, to get rid of it as quickly as possible. At the end of the minister's statement a while ago he said that the federal government were undecided whether to go on with it or not; that especially in view of the fact that the provincial government had gone into the field of investigation it might be better to wait and see what progress the provincial government would make before the dominion government incurred any further expense. Of course that is a very nice way of, shall I say, passing the buck to the province and now withdrawing gracefully from that field. The opportunity seems to have presented itself at the right time. I think the minister said that it would take something like $25 million to build a properly equipped pilot plant; that they were hesitant whether they should spend that money now in view of the provincial government's activity there, and that they would wait and see what the developments were.
Not a pilot plant. A commercial plant.

I would suggest to the minister that, the federal government having

spent a large amount of money without getting anywhere, it would be good business on their part, instead of spending $25 million there in the erection of a commercial plant, to give about $15 million of that amount to the government of Alberta to assist them in their research work. The provincial government of Alberta has an interest in that oil field and is determined to go ahead and see what can be done with it. My information is that satisfactory progress is being made, and I believe it would be a good financial investment and an important contribution for the federal government to give the provincial government $15 million to build a commercial plant. Added to the $250,000 which the province has already put into the operation it could make a worth-while investigation. It would not only help the federal government but aid this country in time of need. We need not bury our heads in the sand and think that all dangers of war have disappeared and that never again will there be a world war. Now is the time for us to begin to prepare ourselves to obtain those things which are necessary to the operation of the war and which were so scarce during that critical time a year ago. It would be both a gesture toward the safety of the country and a good business proposition from the point of view of the dominion if the federal government would give the province $15 million of that amount which they would otherwise have to spend for the erection of a commercial plant to carry on.

The hon. member for Bow River is not quite correct in stating that nothing has resulted from the expenditures of money by the dominion government. I stated, on the strength of a report given by the directors, that the expenditures made bj the Abasand company in carrying out the investigations have clearly shown that the sands can be mined without any serious obstacles even under winter conditions, and with the powerful equipment that we use in large-scale operations no mining difficulties should) be encountered. That was one of the problems they had to solve, and they did.
The investigation has resulted in the development of a new method of separating the bitumen from the sand.
That also had to be demonstrated in some way before the operations on these sands could be accomplished.
This process appears to have definite advantages over the hot water process formerly used, indicating lower costs, increased recoveries of bitumen from the sands and lower loss of the diluent used in the process. It has been shown also that for high recovery of bitumen and' low diluent loss, the feed to the separation plant should consist of freshly mined unoxidized sand.

The minister mentioned three things which the federal government had discovered, one being that now, after this tremendous amount of money has been spent by the Dominion of Canada, it is found that these tar sands cannot be properly worked. A year ago I said that mining was one of the topics being discussed, and after 47696-182
several years of experimentation the federal government decided to employ a man from the United States. That man went there and in a matter of hours he was able to tell the operators how to mine it. The old process was to use machines with cups on them; when they ran against the bank and struck anything granite-like the cups were broken off and their technicians were so good that they did not know how to get around the obstacle. This man simply told them to use a stick of dynamite and blow it loose. That was one of the biggest factors in solving the problem. The other method of separating the liquids was to use either hot water or hydrogenation. It is my information that while the federal government was building its hopes on the hydrogenation process, that was not so practical as even the hot water, and all hon. members will remember that when the Abasand company had tie plant they were using the hot-water method.
One hundred and eighty degrees.

Yes, and in using that method the Abasand company was able to produce 400 barrels a day; but since the federal government started the use of the new method they have not been producing anything, or at any rate a very small quantity. It is true that the plant burned down and that held up operations.
How many times did it burn down?

Once. It was pulled
down once and burned down once. . These are the great discoveries that the federal government has made after the expenditure of over $200,000, or in fact more than that- a million and a half all told. That is rather expensive in view of the results obtained, and it would be much better and more satisfactory if the federal government would get out of the field, which I think they are gracefully trying to do after making such a failure of the venture, and give the provincial government at least half of that $25,000,000 which it would cost them to erect a new commercial plant. We have three trucks going all the time between these different buildings, on business of the department. We need them all, and we need the mechanic to keep the trucks in running order.
Mr. TOWNLEY-SMITH:	What do the

I should like to
obtain from the minister a statement showing the various amounts it is anticipated will be expended in the different provinces under this item. I wish also to ascertain what has been done during the last year, particularly in Saskatchewan, in connection with the exploration or investigation of potential mineral areas. When this vote was up last year I asked this question and pointed out that an insignificant amount was being expended in Saskatchewan, which I think is one province in which something should be done toward providing some complementary industries alongside agriculture. The potential mineral resources are there. The private companies which during the past ten years pursued these investigations ceased those activities during the period of the war because of the demand for the development of areas and in consequence exploratory work was not undertaken by them, having regard to manpower shortages and the like.

If I may interrupt the hon, member, perhaps the information he requires could be given under the vote for geological surveys. This item is for mineral resources investigations, and consists really of laboratory work done here in Ottawa. All mining throughout Canada receives the benefit of what is done here in Ottawa. What the hon. member has been speaking about might come under geological surveys, and I would be able to tell him what was done.
What does come under this head of mineral, resources investigations?

Under this vote are carried on office, laboratory and field investigations relating to metallic minerals, industrial minerals, fuels and mineral economics.
Laboratories are maintained for investigations on small scale and on semi-commercial scale. They are housed in several up-to-date buildings on Booth street, at Lydia street, in the city of Ottawa. The investment in buildings and equipment to December 31, 1943. totalled more than $1,750,000. As a group the laboratories are probably not equalled anywhere. The services provided are in demand by industry to an extent that cannot be met with the existing staff
This has nothing to do with field exploration?
No, except from the general laboratory point of view. Industry gets the benefit of it.
Is the work done by this branch for independent prospectors?
No.
About one-quarter of this item is for temporary assistance. Of what does that consist?
All the labouring staff in the mines laboratories.

Would the minister give us the details of the work which this branch has been doing in the past year? I went through the laboratory a couple of years ago, and I remember that at that time they were doing certain work in connection with coal. Gould we have an idea of the work now being done, or what has been done during 1945?

The anticipated activities for the year 1945-46 are as follows:
Physical metallurgy tests and investigations in reference to the production of war equipment, as required by the Department of National Defence (naval, army and air services), the Department of Munitions and Supply, and British missions in Canada and the United States; tests and investigational work on ores and industrial minerals, some of which are still classed as strategic and required for war use; studies and investigational work on fuels, including hydrogenation, for the coal controller and the royal commission on coal; and specialized economic studies pertaining to minerals and metals.
New premises for investigations in physical metallurgy (with a floor area of 32,345 square feet) were occupied in January, 1944, and to these there is to be an addition, now under construction, for the housing of metal forming equipment so necessary in investigations on the most efficient use of metals. Magnesium metal is likely to be the first one investigated.
Funds having been provided for a new hydrogenation laboratory, to produce about 200 gallons of gasoline a day, a considerable proportion of the time of the fuels division staff will necessarily be given to interior design of the building and the equipment to be housed therein.

133. Geological surveys, $341,000.
Is this the item under which my question should have been asked?

Yes. The hon. member for Lake Centre asked a question, the answer to which would come under this vote. Vote 132 is to provide for the administration of the bureau of geology and topography. This is to provide for administration of the bureau of geology and topography; the maintenance of a national aerial photographic library, studies arising therefrom and interpretations from aerial photographs for industry; the operation of a photographic laboratory for the performance of work related to map making and other branch activities; and 'the maintenance , and operation of the geological survey library (upward of 80,000 volumes). Then the hon. member for Lake Centre was asking as to the survey field parties in 1945-46. In the northwest territory there were five parties; in the Yukon and Northwest Territories, one; on the Yukon and Alaska highway, one; in British Columbia, seven; in Alberta, five; in Saskatchewan and Alberta, one; in Saskatchewan, two; in Manitoba, three; in Ontario, two; in Quebec, six; in New Brunswick, one; in Nova Scotia, two; various provinces, one. In all there were thirty-seven survey parties.
Do they still confine themselves to surface work?

Then, the topographical field survey, 1945-46: vote 134, number of parties in
Yukon and British Columbia, two; Northwest Territories, one; Alberta, four; Manitoba, one; Quebec, one; New Brunswick, one; Nova Scotia, two. This makes a total of twelve.

Is there to-day any activity in the minister's branch leading to exploratory work which is taking place with a view to ascertaining where minerals are located.
Under the report of the reconstruction council, one of the activities which the government intended to undertake, with a view to providing employment, was exploratory work to be carried on as part of the general scheme of rehabilitation.
Is any provision being made by the minister's department for the training of men returning from overseas as prospectors, and the sending out of these prospecting parties in order to improve the economy? I have in mind particularly the province of Saskatchewan, where preliminary investigations have shown tremendous mineral wealth, which must be developed as a result of leadership from the' federal government. It will not be developed provincially because the responsibility primarily must fall on the dominion government in any national scheme of rehabilitation. We in Saskatchewan have found ourselves in the position that during the war very little was spent in our province for industrial development. Only a few industries were opened.
With the coming of peace we are returning once again to an agricultural economy, although investigations show that our mineral wealth is such that with proper leadership from the department much could be done toward expanding our economy so as to include a mineral economy, with a consequent advantage to the province and to the dominion as a . whole. I make the plea to the minister, because in recent years Saskatchewan has been left out of the picture in regard to industrial development, not only by his department but generally. If the government would undertake the ascertainment of the areas and the general location of areas peculiarly fitted to potential mineral development, it might well improve the economy of the province and assure a greater measure of employment and self-sufficiency in that direction.

I have listened with interest to what the hon. member has said. As he may know, we have had great difficulty in getting geologists because, like other staffs, our staff has been depleted owing to the loss of men. Men are not being educated in this profession in sufficient numbers that we may hope in the immediate future to have many
Supply-Mines and Resources

additional geologists whom we can, send out into the field. This is a matter of great concern to the department and has been the subject of a good many conversations. What the hon. gentleman has said with regard to the post-war period is certainly ever present in the minds of the officers of my department.

I should like to refer briefly to the Merritt district in British Columbia. I have on my desk two publications of the department under the minister's jurisdiction, one dated 1905 and the other 1915. I requested the department to let me have the 'latest information about surveys made in that area and they sent me a number of publications. These are the only ones in which any reference is made to the district. The first quotation I should like to make is from a report by an official of the department at that time, Doctor R. W. Ells, who made a survey of the Nicola coal basin in British Columbia. I should like to quote from page 47A of this report of 1905 as follows:
The length of the main coal basin of the Nicola-Cold water area, from the foot of Nicola lake to the south limit on the Coldwater, in a southwest direction, is about ten miles, and the greatest breadth is about three miles. The western portion, from the forks of the Cold-water to the volcanics of Ten Mile creek or Lower Nicola, is about five miles, with an extension, north and south, along the creeks of about ten miles. The length of the eastern or Quil-chena basin is about seven miles from north to south and the maximum breadth apparently about two and a half miles.
We have it established there that there is a substantial potential coal field in that area. The point I intend to make by my further quotation is that the surveys made of the area were never completed. Discussing the lay of the land, Doctor Ells says, as reported on page 48A of the same report:
Unfortunately, of several borings made during the season of 1904, none succeeded in penetrating the drift, and as the underlying rock was hot reached, no light was afforded as to the structure of this part of the basin.
I quote only to show that there was established the presence of a coal field, but the report is not conclusive as to the economic value. In the report of 1915 Doctor Camsell is reported on page 281 as saying.
The importance of the district about Merritt depends primarily on the presence of oligocene rocks containing bituminous coals.
There were further reports on the coal seams which were found in that area, the thickness of one being reported as Toeing thirteen feet six inches. But again no sufficient

survey appears to have been made, and we find Doctor Ells reporting again on page 284 as follows:
In view of the widespread nature of the drift throughout the entire area the actual economic value of these areas can only be ascertained by a number of bore holes.
Further on in the same report he makes the statement that unfortunately none of those further surveys were made. From time to time a number of small mines have operated in that area, but none of them had sufficiently large financial resources behind them to make exhaustive surveys. While this was not the responsibility of the minister, during the war period certain directives were issued by the emergency coal production board. Admittedly that board was not concerned with the small operator; their main concern was to get the largest body of coal out as efficiently as they could. Nevertheless, owing in part to the directives issued by that board, one of the mines operating in that area was closed down.
This operator has undertakings that if he can show the presence of k large body of coal in that area he can interest other capital in the Merritt area and possibly start his mine again now that labour is becoming available. However, as I say, no complete survey has been made, and this man has not at his disposal sufficient capital to undertake the survey himself. I should like to make the same plea as was made by the hon. member for Lake Centre. At oie time this was a prosperous community. There is the established presence of a large body of coal in that area. At present the area is largely agricultural and it requires some other industry to produce a balanced economy. I should like the minister to allocate some of these moneys so that an exhaustive geological survey of that area can be made to find out the potential economic resources of the coal fields there.

I have listened to the hon. gentleman, but again may I say that our trouble is lack of expert men to cover the field. This is a large field, but I have noted what the hon. gentleman says and will give consideration to it.
Geological surveys?
I want data of the last geological survey, together with any revisions that have since been made.
There were two altogether,.one in Goldfields, a rare element investigation, and the other in Rotten Stone lake, in connection with metallic minerals.
What was the date?
This summer, 1945.
Has a general geological survey been made of the northern part of Saskatchewan and is the data completed? -
Just a portion of it.
Are maps available?

I should like to say one word in connection with the suggestion of the hon. member for Lake Centre, who asked if it was the intention of the government to train some of our returned men as prospectqrs in our northern regions. If that is to be done we should see that our returned men who act as prospectors receive better remuneration than prospectors have received in the past. It is very important that we should train men to act as mining prospectors; it will mean much to the development of the country, and I know of no class that have contributed more to the development of mining than the prospectors. It is doubtful if there is any other group that has received less remuneration for the work they have done. It is up to the department to lay early plans whereby our
prospectors will receive more remuneration than they have received in the important industry of mining.

Item agreed to.
Lands, parks and forests branch-
IS7. Branch administration, $20,090.

Before the war there was a disposition on the part of the dominion government to put up dollar for dollar with the provinces for the purpose of building connecting roads from the international boundary to the provincial highways, largely for the purpose of enabling tourists to reach the parks. I should like the minister to tell the committee whether that is now in contemplation once more, because a good deal of interest is being taken in the tourist movement and a good deal of money has been spent in advertising the tourist business. It will certainly be of great assistance in British Columbia to get tourists from the various entry points on the international boundary up into the park.

Post-war work and projects will be duly considered, and one that will certainly come up for consideration will be the building of roads leading to our parks to invite and encourage the tourist traffic.
It is not covered by this item?
No.

I should like to say a few words about our national parks under this item. I am particularly interested in it, because for many years I have been in a business in which I have been closely in contact with people who visit our parks from year to year and I have been very much impressed with their reports. I am prompted to speak on this item particularly as it relates to the tourist traffic.
On November 7 of this year, a Mr. A. O. Seymour, of Montreal, speaking at a meeting of the members of the Canadian Association of Tourists and Publicity Bureaux, predicted that some 26,000,000 United States anglers and hunters with more than four billion dollars to spend annually on their hobbies will be in the North American tourist market within a few years. This figure may or may not be exaggerated; I hope it is true, and in support of that I was pleased indeed to see a statement made by the minister of health at the same meeting outlining a new programme of federal activity in the tourist field, including the further development of our national parks. That is a commendable project. I do not think we can go too far in the expansion of
Supply-Mines and Resources

our national parks across Canada, because they are so closely linked with the great tourist industry. I should like to bring before the members of the house some important facts which I believe will be of interest. Often we are tempted to become more or less complacent and sit back and think someone else will do the work. We do not regard our parks as important as they really are.
From a small beginning nearly sixty years ago Canada's national parks have expanded until to-day there are some twenty-six parks beckoning visitors to every province. They contain about 30,000 square miles, all under federal ownership and administration, and they are fairly well spread across Canada, with four in British Columbia, six in Alberta, one in Saskatchewan, two in Manitoba, five in Ontario, two in Quebec, one in New Brunswick, one in Prince Edward Island and four in Nova Scotia. In addition, I am told that recently gome 10,000 square miles have been set aside adjacent to the Alaska highway in the Yukon territory, as well as two sites offered by the province of Quebec and one by the province of New Brunswick. I believe that discussions are proceeding at the present time for a national park to be located partly in the province of Ontario in my own constituency of Leeds and partly in New York state. If it becomes a reality it will to a great extent be unique, and with its beautiful setting be another link in this great chain of show places across Canada. I hope to have more to say about that later on. Our present system of parks, even without these proposed extensions, is one of the finest and largest in the world. The parks include regions of outstanding beauty, natural phenomena, historic sites, wild bird and animal life. They conserve the country's wild creatures under natural conditions, and provide places for vacationing, no matter in what phase of outdoor life the visitor may be interested. There is, however, a great lack of accommodation in some of these parks for the casual visitor of moderate means, and also a shortage of small roadside parks with sanitary and cooking facilities.
I submit that more small parks should be established. If I may use for example my own constituency of Leeds, there is the famous chain of Itideau lakes. People travel thousands of miles to fish and hunt and enjoy the beautiful scenery, but absolutely no national park exists in the area where tourists can feel free to recuperate and receive the hospitality of our people. In the area there are several ideal spots suitable for small, well-equipped parks, and I am sure there are many such

places across Canada. I hope the government will give some consideration to these matters at the earliest opportunity.
To bring out my point, which is the importance of increasing the number of these parks across Canada, and especially the upkeep of those already in use, I am going again to refer to my own St. Lawrence islands national parks, principally located in my own constituency of Leeds. One of the most picturesque regions on the north American continent is the fifty-mile stretch of the St. Lawrence river between Kingston and Brockville. Along this section of great inland waterways its waters are studded with upwards of 1,700 beautiful islands varying in size from less than an acre to several square miles, and separated one from another by picturesque channels. These islands are clothed with groves of pine, oak, maple and birch, which rise above the bluffs of granite and limestone to cast shadows and deeper colour across the emerald waters. Nature has undoubtedly created here one of her masterpieces in river landscape.
For nearly three-quarters of a century the Thousand Islands, as they are called, have been a paradise for the summer visitor, so much so that most of the islands are now privately owned. However, as early as 1904 the* government of Canada in their wisdom set aside as national recreational areas a number of these islands which now form the St. Lawrence Islands national park. AJt the present time the park is composed of thirteen islands accessible from rivers and towns along the St. 'Lawrence river and mainland area at Mallorytown landing. On many of these islands improvements have been carried out and conveniences provided for visitors. Attractively designed pavilions and shelters have been erected, outdoor camp stoves, tables, benches, and, as a rule, firewood provided, and wharves and boat landings constructed to facilitate approach. Several of these islands have bathing beaches, and excellent fishing may be enjoyed in the surrounding waters. These parks have for many years supplied recreation for thousands of people from many countries. From my summer camp I am able to see three of the islands which form this group of parks, and therefore I have a first-hand impression of the activity about them. Hundreds of boats anchor at the wharves, some just overnight, some for days, some for weeks, and many times when they are caught in a storm. Believe me, I have a pretty fair idea of the value of such parks in the St. Lawrence.
Having said this, I wish to bring before this committee the deplorable condition of these

Supply-Mines and Resources
parks and docks at the present time. I believe the same condition applies to several of these parks across Canada. I do not offer this, to any great extent at least, in the way of criticism, because I am cognizant of the shortage of material and labour during the war years, also the high water which' has taken its toll in the way of heavy damage to wharves. However, now that hostilities have ceased, I submit that no time should be lost in restoring these parks and wharves to their original usefulness and beauty. I believe this is urgent for, as I see it, we must be ready to receive and provide recreation and entertainment for the vast numbers of visitors moving from one province to another, and the tremendous influx of people from other countries which we are bound to have very shortly, now that the condition of peace again exists.
We' must not look, at this great tourist industry purely from a monetary point of view; we must meet these people with a sense of genuine welcome, and treat them in a realistic manner while they are our guests. Our national parks were established, in the words of one of our great statesmen, "to recuperate our people and to recoup our treasury." Let there be no possibility of , misunderstandings, but let the greatest sense of friendship prevail with these people from all provinces and from all lands.
In conclusion, may I say that all across Canada nature has provided us with the most beautiful settings in the world for national parks and playgrounds-gifts that cannot be set by hands-and no government can or will sit idly by and allow any of these parks to deteriorate when a nominal expenditure will keep up and expand these beautiful show places that present a "welcome" to people of our own country, and particularly to people from other countries, which will leave with them a lasting remembrance of the greatest country on God's green earth-Canada!
Some time during the discussion I am sure the minister will be good enough to comment on the suggestions which I have made.

Just
before we leave this item I should like to ask the minister a question. Does the federal government give any assistance for the development of our provincial parks, and, if not, is there any contemplated under dominion-provincial agreement?

The best answer I can give the hon. member who has just spoken and to the hon. member for Leeds is to read a paragraph from the reference book for the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction with which I agree:
The matter of coordinating dominion and provincial activities in the development of interprovincial and international tourist travel, mainly by means of establishing adequate graded facilities for the use of tourists; the development of national and provincial parks to the highest point of attractiveness consistent with the principles of conservation upon which they are based; and the devising and financing of publicity campaigns representing the experience and interests not only of the dominion but of all the provincial units, surely presents a large and profitable field to be studied and explored by all the interests concerned.
I can assure hon. gentlemen and the committee that the department is keen on establishing parks wherever possible. There is nothing it will not do to encourage such an establishment of parks in any of the provinces of Canada, knowing of course that the land must be surrendered and be given to the dominion by the provinces, and the dominion will then have charge of it. I know from my experience of Riding Mountain park in my own constituency the benefits of a national park to the whole of Manitoba. In particular, I know what an attraction it is to United States tourists. We are getting more and more of them all the time, and I am hoping that in the post-war period we shall have further attempts to make our parks so attractive that our tourist trade will be one of the biggest industries in Canada.
As to the first part of my question-?
No assistance is given to provincial parks.

Could the minister give information as to what national parks there are in Ontario, where they are, what the acreage is, and to what extent the parks department of the federal government cooperate with that of the provincial government?

There are three parks: Point Pelee, Ontario. Recreational area on lake Erie, with fine beaches and unique flora. Resting point for migratory birds. Established 1918; area, 6-04 square miles. Georgian Bay islands, Ontario. Thirty islands in Georgian bay. Unique formations on flowerpot island. Recreational area. Established 1929; area, 5-37 square miles. St. Lawrence islands, Ontario. Mainland area, and thirteen islands in "Thousand Islands" group with recreational facilities. Reserved 1904; established 1914; area, 185-6 acres. Then there are the historic sites, but that is not the question.

Can the minister give us the numbers that have gone through the national parks in the past year?
I shall have to get that information.

While the deputy is getting that information, I would urge the minister, on behalf of Ontario, to give a little more eonsideration to the province so far as park sites are concerned. I do not believe that the parks described by the minister are anything like the extent that they should be in a province bordering on the United States, with the vast number of tourists passing through Ontario. I believe it would greatly benefit not only Ontario but the dominion as well if a much greater effort were made by the department at Ottawa to foster tourist trade and sports of various kinds in Ontario, by the establishment of -many more national parks than we have now and also by greater cooperation with the province in the direction of tourists to Ontario. We have a large area near to the United States, bordering on the great centres of that country, and it would be a profitable investment if the dominion were to do much more than it has done so far, because I do not believe that the dominion government has done its proper share in the establishment and maintenance of parks in Ontario in comparison with other provinces. If you calculate the acreage and the expenditures made in other provinces and compare those figures with similar figures in Ontario you will find that it has been pretty well left to the Ontario government to maintain our national parks. There are many places in the province where national parks could be established which would be a real source of revenue to the people of Canada as well as to the residents of Ontario. I should like the minister to give that point his consideration.

The hon. member knows that for any national park to be established in Ontario the land must be offered by the province to the dominion. I will consider what he has said in this regard. As regards the question asked by the hon. member for Souris, I have here a list of parks, with attendance. Would it be in order for me to put that list on Hansard, or do hon. members wish to have me read it?
I would be willing to have it put on Hansard. It would give useful information.

I have extensive notes, Mr. Chairman, and I wish to say something about national parks, but since I do not want to be accused of reading my speech I may say that my notes are: "Banff National park, Indians, fish." I gather that Indians come a little later, so that I will give my notes to the hon. member for Lake Centre and he will work on them tonight and do a good job on them to-morrow. What I intend to say is in a sense critical, but I begin by thanking the minister and his staff for meeting the hon. member for Calgary East and myself shortly after I came here and being very generous to us with the information which they had. I spent two hours very profitably with Mr. Smart yesterday, or perhaps Saturday, and I wish to say how much I appreciate the honest endeavour which was made to answer the questions that were given to me to ask by those persons who reside at Banff. Banff being in my constituency-and I hope they are all listening- I have to say something on their behalf.
I think it fair to make this criticism. I realize thoroughly that during the war period there was little opportunity for the dominion government to do anything for that park,.

Supply-Mines and Resources
and I assume that had equal application elsewhere. I have looked through these estimates and have sought in vain, although perhaps I missed it, for some assistant* to tourist traffic; and that applies, I think, generally to all the parks we have.
It has been well said that tourists are becoming perhaps our second major industry. It may be that I have overlooked the vote; if so, we will cover it at the proper time. AVith respect to Banff, it is in close proximity to the place where I live and have lived for a long time. It is a place I have gone to often, and its transformation in recent years is something of which this parliament might well take .cognizance. I mean this. Years ago these places were summer resorts, but that day has gone. To-day it is impossible to get *even a room in which one may live in Banff, as a result of the introduction of this new art called in Norway "She-ing", but which,I prefer to describe by our own expression- skiing.

You do not use combinations in skis. The hon. gentleman has an old pair of spring skates. Standing by this hotel over here yesterday, Sunday-that of course will not be appreciated by Quebec and Ontario members because none of them are here then-I watched people disgorging from that place by hundreds-and you have not enough snow to fill a hollow tooth. Nevertheless they were enjoying themselves. So that winter and summer these parks of ours are an asset which the department- and I 'say this with great respect-has so far failed to appreciate fully.
I mention in these extensive notes which, as I said a moment ago. I gave to the hon. member for Lake Centre, the business of fish, and here I do criticize the administration of the parks. AA7e have a fish hatchery at Banff, the only one in that- park. They have endeavoured to cover a great deal of territory. It may be they were assisted by the government of-Alberta ; I do not know. However, I have been fishing for a long time, and I have no unkind remarks to make to you fellows who fish with live minnow's or frogs or worms or anything of that sort, but you do miss the most scientific thing in the world, next to golf or billiards; that is, to cast a proper fly in a proper spot. I have been in Kamloops, from which my young friend over here comes, though he has been here for months and has not even mentioned this, and there they have the greatest fly-fishing the world knows. AVe should have it on this side of the Rocky mountains. AVhy do wp not? Because in the
Banff national park sufficient attention has not been paid to it. One need only study the number of licences issued to fishermen in the United States to see what an immense attraction it would be; but as a federal department we have been using only that little hatchery.
It has been working hard, and is operated by splendid people, but we have been supplying fish to other portions of Alberta which should be looked after by the province.
Let us go along a step further. I hope no one will think I am talking nonsense while speaking of fish in the House of Commons, because I know how stupid and foolish fishermen are supposed to be, since I am one of them myself. AA7e will go miles and miles in order to drop a fly in a certain spot; then things happen, and who knows who shall succeed?

maintopic: STATEMENT OF ATTENDANCE AT THE NATIONAL PARKS
speechtext:
How long are they?
Mr, SMITH (Calgary West): Perhaps I had better answer that question. In Peter Hope lake, thirty-five miles north of Kamloops, you can take Kamloops trout just about the length my hon. friend indicated; they will weigh six pounds and. you can get them on the fly. In one afternoon my wife and I took six fish weighing thirty and a half pounds. That was the greatest afternoon of my life, not excepting the time I have spent in this parliament. But come over to our side of the mountains and it is different, with the exception of one lake where you pack forty-two miles-and that is a big t.w6 days' pack-and where you can catch three-pound cutthroats. Other than that I know of no place outside of the mountains where you can catch any fish, certainly no place that can be approached by people who drive a motor car and like to catch a fish or two. Just before coming here in September, my wife and I packed with the greatest guide in the world, a man by the name of Jim Boyce, into the Skoki country. We fished Baker lake and Red Deer lake. The fish in Baker lake were about the size indicated by my hon. friend a moment ago. We caught quite a number, but. nothing over two pounds. The answer is very simple; it is failure to have regard to feed conditions, and to stock according to them. The hon. member for Kamloops will know that about eight.y-fite miles south of his city-I almost called it a town- there is a lake called' Penask lake where a man by the name of Dole, the pineapple Dole, built a club. I was foolish enough to join at $50 a year, which meant that the fish 1 caught cost me about $50 a pound.
In that part of the country we have the greatest opportunity to attract tourists. It has been often figured out that tourists-and

Supply-Mines and Resources
I do not care whether they come in a jalopy or in a big car-leave about 87 per day per person, and that goes to our people here engaged in feeding them, selling gasoline, bedding people down and all that sort of thing. I would wish that the department might get a new inspiration, might have vision to see this grand picture, this great thing that may be done. Some of you bait fishermen may say. well, once you make these places available, then you fish them out and there are no fish left. I can give an example to prove that statement completely wrong. Twelve miles north of Kamloops there is a little lake twelve miles long and not more that three-quarters of a mile wide a(t any point. It has been intensively fished for thirty odd years. The commission in British Columbia regard that lake and call it their test tube, for the reason that they know pretty well the approximate number of fish that come out, and the number of fish they put in. As I say, it has been intensively fished for thirty odd years; I have been there for fifteen years without a single break. You can catch fish on the fly there roughly from May 24 to the end of the second week in June and then again after September 15. I wish the hon. member for Davenport were here, because he would take you up one side of that lake and down the other without missing a single tree as he went along. I mention that particular lake, because the theory that lakes get fished out is quite true if you do not restock. That lake is restocked by the British Columbia authorities. Try to get a room there this summer; you will fail unless you have made reservations a long time ahead.
I am going back now to the town of Banff; and may I say that with a new minister I trust we shall have a new inspiration with respect to our national parks. These remarks are not made in criticism of Mr. Smart or any of those other gentlemen associated with him.
I know what their difficulties are. When a man sets up a business in Banff he goes to live in the cheapest place in the world. He does not pay very much for his lot, on which he gets a long lease. Now you have a town planner who is going to make it a city beautiful, or something like that. A building will be torn down there; a sign will be taken off over there, and I know it is going to be wonderful. But we have there what is called an advisory council, which was formed when the late Sir James Lougheed was minister of the interior and that place came under his department. I have spent some time with those people in Banff. My hon. friends to my left will be happy to know, I am sure, that 
more of the people of Banff voted for me than all the other candidates put together, and there were four against me there-so that I am very happy to tell you what wonderful people they are.
I hope that the minister, inspired as he will be with his new job and the great future that opens before him, will do something, though frankly I am unable to tell what to do, to end the dissatisfaction that exists as between the local council and the government officials. I am not criticizing Mr. P. J. Jennings, a very old friend who is the superintendent, but I am sure this thing has become so big that you cannot operate the Banff national park from two thousand miles away. There must be a little more delegation of authority and more active cooperation given those who have been elected by their people and who think they know something about the problems of Banff.
May I put it in this way. I am not suggesting that they are right; I do not know. I know they have grievances, although I am inclined to think thus will apply to other parts as well. They may be wrong. I am happy to learn that Mr. Smart is going out there in February. Yesterday I was able to write them and say, "You have put all this on my shoulders, but Mr. Smart will be there in February, so jump on his back and see how you get along with him." I told them what a delightful gentleman he was-and of course they already knew it. But I told him to take the matter up with them.
That is what I am trying to get at. I do think-well, I do not even think; I know that parks are a national problem, because of the tourist traffic. I know that the department wants to get United States dollars, and the department has done something. It has joined with the province of Alberta in building two highways leading to Banff national park. It seems to me a liaison could be arranged, through the hon. member who leads the Social Credit party. Let us have a lot more of that partnership, by which even now so much has been done. And yet it is so little, having regard to the main objective.
The complaint to-day in Banff is that you cannot get a lot, or lease one, under any circumstances. I appreciate the minister's difficulties. Water services and light services have to be laid on. I know that the minister is giving this sympathetic consideration, and that the veterans affairs committee-and the Minister of Veterans Affairs knows all about this-made a splendid recommendation the other day to the Minister of Mines and Re-

Privilege-Mr. Tucker
sources. Our returned chaps have not a chance there, because the assistance which is given in other places really has no application. However, I know that those are little difficulties which will be ironed out.
Now, having talked about fish-and I am not joking; I know how important it is; there is not any doubt about that-

speechtext: Go ahead.

maintopic: STATEMENT OF ATTENDANCE AT THE NATIONAL PARKS
speechtext: I will be only a minute or two-but perhaps I had better stop there. I might get my second wind if I were permitted to go on.

Very well; it is eleven o'clock. Perhaps to-morrow morning at eleven o'clock you will hear something, Mr. Chairman.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
It being five minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, December 4, 1945.
